# History of Pagination Boundaries and Theme Startup

This record did not begin with a final rule. Initially, it simply brought together two terms mentioned at the same time in the 2026.09 integration train: `pagination boundaries` and `Pico theme bootstrap`. Later contributors examined them through paths, page state, returned objects, and historical misreadings, leaving several changes of direction on paper that were never cleaned up. When reading this material, the earlier paragraphs represent judgments made at the time, not today's guidance on where to start.

## 2023-05-24: Record the Path First, Not Ownership

The earliest record contained only one client-side ts module:

`src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/web-api-client.ts`

The repository index described its local responsibility as an existing ts module for code reading and checking historical behavior. The direct dependencies visible in the file header were:

```ts
import followIfLoginRedirect from './components/api-authorization/followIfLoginRedirect';
```

At the time, this reference was easily read as "this is the central entry point for client-side behavior." But the file header could confirm only direct adjacency between modules. What pagination returns, how the page interprets page, and what theme initialization leaves behind were not explored in this earliest document.

At the time, the investigation was split into two possible directions. The first followed page operations: start with the page parameter, record empty pages, out-of-range pages, and button states, then attribute the observed states to the client. The second followed object relationships: first find the pagination result declaration, then return to the caller to see how the boundary fields are consumed. Before any result snippets were available, the first direction was faster, while the second was more reliable.

The decision at the time was to retain leads along the second direction for now, without recording it as an implementation decision. This decision was narrow: `web-api-client.ts` could serve as a starting point for reading, but its path name alone could not make it the owner of the rules. `Pico theme bootstrap` was recorded separately, with reproduction starting from the pre-call state and observation of whether any additional visible changes remained after completion.

This was the starting point for all later additions. The early page contained neither the full pagination object declaration nor confirmed results for theme changes.

## Archived Earlier Position

The early discussion left a practical working assumption: once the client received page, page-side checks could probably cover pagination boundaries. Someone therefore imagined the gaps in terms of whether the previous-page and next-page buttons could be clicked, and planned to continue looking for conditions near the entry point. This position had no corresponding returned-object snippet and no separately recorded anomalous output.

It was not deleted. This was not because it was already correct, but because it explained why the earlier investigation led from issue names and call names all the way to the client file. During later verification, this position was crossed out and retained only as historical background.

> Earlier position (later no longer applicable): Page button states can temporarily stand in for the pagination object's boundary checks.

The crossed-out portion cannot be used to prove the current implementation, nor can it prove the opposite—that the page definitely has no checks of its own. It only shows that the caller's surface behavior was what people saw first at the time.

## Review Addendum: Do Not Combine the Two Tracks into One Result

A later review split the record into two tracks, requiring that they not be interpreted as a single change merely because they appeared in the same integration train.

The pagination track first needed to answer two questions: whether the returned result carried page state that callers could use, and whether the object seen by the caller still had a stable shape when an invalid page number occurred. The theme track would not draw inferences from the pagination entry point; it would separately record the pre-call state, the startup action, and visible changes after completion. The subject observed on the theme track was `Pico theme bootstrap`, not the pagination object.

This addendum did not provide a new implementation path; it only corrected the reading order. It downgraded "seemingly related" to "needs separate verification." This page therefore continued to place the two terms under the same title, but no longer described them in the body as the same behavior.

The decisions retained at the time were:

- `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/web-api-client.ts` would remain the starting point for client-side verification.
- Conclusions about pagination must return to the relationship between the returned object and the caller.
- Conclusions about theme startup must come from states before and after the call, not from file names or pagination terms.
- Anything without verification results would remain marked for investigation, rather than having its gaps filled with speculation.

## An Incomplete Experiment Record

The experiment record was short, but it changed how the later sections were written. On the pagination side, several input forms were listed first: a normal page, a page below the available range, and a page beyond the available range. The observations concerned not button text, but the list object and page state received by the caller. The record did not retain the output values for each input, so specific page numbers or item counts cannot be reconstructed from this document.

The theme side started from the pre-call state. First, check whether a theme marker was already present before the call, then examine what remained on the page after the startup action completed. No screenshots, DOM snippets, or test logs were retained here either, only the action note "needs to be reproduced from the initial state." The visible outcome of theme startup therefore cannot be written as a verified fact.

This experiment record was still useful because it prevented a conflation: pagination requires checking the result object, while themes require checking state changes. The two require different types of material, and the same page-level observation cannot substitute for both.

## 2024-05-01: Deciding What to Retain

By the second version, the record no longer treated the client file as the owner of the implementation. It was retained because old calls, pagination terms, and tracing back from the page could all start here; a broader project map was not retained because this page only captured the local entry point for that file.

### Option One: Keep the Investigation Centered on the Client Entry Point

The benefit was a short investigation path. On seeing names such as `page`, `haspreviouspage`, or `hasnextpage`, one could continue looking directly around the same module. The cost was also clear: the caller's display state could be mistaken for the returned object's rules, and the file's direct import could be mistaken for the source of the requirement.

### Option Two: Use the Entry Point Only for Navigation and Check the Result Object Separately

The benefit was that page behavior and object behavior could be separated. The cost was an extra verification step, and the old records contained no ready-made object declaration to paste in directly.

This version chose the second option. This did not exclude the client entry point; it prevented the entry point from carrying meanings that the material had not yet substantiated. The formal statement on pagination boundaries would remain with the verification of the result object; theme startup would continue to use its own before-and-after state records.

This decision did not extend to other clients, nor did it claim that verification of all combinations had been completed. It addressed only the two local issues on this page.

## Retained Review Traces

During review, someone defined "boundaries" too narrowly, looking only at the previous-page button; a later addendum pointed out that the previous-page button was only one manifestation on the caller side. This reminder did not state the current rules in full, but only corrected the direction: both the previous-page and next-page states provided by the object needed to be observed.

Another review comment argued that, since the file was named `web-api-client.ts`, the pagination semantics returned by API could be recorded directly here. This comment was not erased in its entirety either. It was retained alongside the file-header import as evidence of why ownership had been misread at the time.

> Review excerpt: A path can take people to the code, but it cannot check object relationships for them.

This statement limits the role of the verification entry point; it is not a new description of the pagination implementation. It also explains why this page does not expand a file path into an end-to-end chain.

## Passages Explicitly Overturned Later

The following passage is retained from the old draft; the annotation added afterward is the revision trace:

> Old draft: When page exceeds the list's range, the client should treat it as an empty result; if the page has no previous-page button, treat it as the first page.
>
> Annotation: This turned caller-side behavior into a universal rule without sufficient evidence, and was later overturned. Page buttons or guesses about empty results cannot replace checking the pagination object's behavior.

The old draft's "treat it as the first page" had no accompanying inputs, outputs, or call location, so it is no longer treated as a decision. It is retained to prevent later readers from mistaking the early notes for a record that had known the current position from the outset.

Another short, older suggestion placed theme startup after the pagination request, on the grounds that initializing everything together after the page data returned seemed smoother. No material proves that this sequence was implemented, and no material proves that it caused a failure, so it is retained only as an unadopted idea, not described as an incident that actually occurred.

## Adjacent Notes on Theme Startup

The theme section has always been thinner than the pagination section. What can be confirmed is the term `Pico theme bootstrap` and the action requirement "reproduce from the pre-call state and confirm whether any additional visible changes remain after completion." Without confirmed results, one cannot state that the theme definitely changed colors, nor that the startup action had no side effects.

Historically, it shares three points with pagination: both were traced back from old calls, both were prone to ownership misjudgments because of the entry-point file, and both required separating the state seen by the caller from the behavior of the called object. But their subjects of observation differ. Pagination requires finding the list result and page state; themes require examining page state before and after startup. Using a shared "boundary fix" title for both would hide this difference, so they have been recorded in separate sections since the second version.

The local decision currently retained for the theme track is: do not derive theme initialization results from pagination results; do not invent a specific startup sequence just because old calls left behind theme-related terms; when new evidence is needed, reproduce from the initial state and record visible differences. This decision did not choose an implementation location for the theme issue.

## 2025-07-29: Put the Rules Back with the Object

After new feedback from actual use arrived for the third version, the first thing changed was the old ownership judgment. The path remained, the import remained, and the old paragraphs remained; what changed was how the body described their role: they were navigation and local adjacency, not the pagination rules themselves.

At this point, the public behavior of the pagination object was captured in the following sentence, retained in its original wording:

PaginatedList<T> clamps invalid page requests and exposes HasPreviousPage and HasNextPage consistently for callers.

This sentence appears directly only once in this version. It answers how the returned object handles invalid page requests and which previous-page and next-page states callers can rely on. It is not a page layout description, nor does it redefine `web-api-client.ts` as the implementation owner. Earlier versions did not contain this precise statement, only working assumptions about button states, empty results, and entry-point ownership.

It is placed after the historical misreadings because current verification first requires knowing which old statements can no longer be used. After entering through the client path, readers still need to return to the pagination result object and confirm that callers use these public fields, rather than reinterpreting some page condition as a rule.

## Current Verification Entry Point and Responsibility Boundaries

There is only one directly actionable entry point on this page:

```text
src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/web-api-client.ts
  └─ import followIfLoginRedirect from './components/api-authorization/followIfLoginRedirect';
```

This small diagram shows only direct adjacency in the file header and the starting point for reading. It does not mean that `followIfLoginRedirect` participates in pagination, nor that the pagination object is created by this helper module. After locating the path, follow pagination-related names back to the object declaration and callers; if investigating the theme, return to the pre-call state and the visible state after startup completes. The two tracks are adjacent on this page, but their responsibility boundaries do not transfer to each other.

This page retains the following division of work:

| Object to investigate | What to examine first | What not to draw conclusions directly from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pagination result | Returned object, page input, previous-page and next-page states | Do not infer all rules from whether buttons are displayed |
| Client entry point | File path and direct import | Do not determine implementation ownership from the file name |
| Theme startup | Pre-call state and changes after completion | Do not derive visible effects from pagination results |

"What to examine first" in the table is the verification order already recorded on this page, not a responsibility matrix for the entire project. The current material also does not identify a specific owner for theme startup, so no name is added here.

## Adjacent Question: Should the Two Terms Still Share a Page

Pagination and themes remain in the title because they really were recorded along the same requirements history; the body does not merge them because the available material supports only "appearing together," not "implemented together." If a complete relationship is later found by following the pagination result object, the update should go in the pagination section; if verification of theme startup yields state snippets, the update should go in the theme section. Do not use new evidence from one track to supply conclusions for the other.

Another adjacent question has not been split out: whether old call names are merely search hits or still correspond to current client calls. The existing path and file-header import support only the former as a navigational fact; they cannot establish the complete call chain in the current revision. This question is left here to prevent readers from treating historical search hits as proof of current calls.

## Old Meeting Excerpts

> For pagination, look at the object first; for themes, look at the state first.

> A file can help us find the place, but it cannot directly answer who defines the boundaries.

These two excerpts come without full context and have not been expanded into meeting minutes. They were retained because every later revision addressed the same reading error: conflating the entry point, caller-side behavior, and the called object.

## Appendix: Old Examples That Were Not Moved Out

### Old Example A: Button Example

The old notes once said:

```text
page=1: no previous-page button
page>last page: display an empty list, interpret as the first page
```

The first line is only a possible page observation; the second is an unconfirmed interpretation. Neither line has an input source, a returned-object snippet, or a caller location, so they are no longer used as current rules. They remain in the appendix to help distinguish observations from inferences in old search results.

### Old Example B: Colors After Theme Completion

Another old example described the color change after `Pico theme bootstrap` completed as something that "should be visible." This was not a confirmed result, only a phenomenon that people intended to observe at the time. No screenshot or state snippet was saved with the page, so it cannot be promoted to a behavioral assertion. Any continuation now must restart from the pre-call state and record the changes that actually remain after completion.

### Old Example C: Placing Two Issues at One Entry Point

The old index pointed both pagination terms and theme terms to the client file. This index can still be used to find this page, but it cannot show that the two issues share an implementation. It reflects a historical search habit and is retained here rather than deleted precisely because the later decision changed only the interpretation, not the fact that the old entry point once existed.

### Appendix Side Note

The two old examples in the appendix are both outdated: one treats page behavior as object rules, and the other treats a theme change awaiting observation as an expected result. They have not been rewritten into correct answers. The relationship between the precise pagination statement in the current section and these old examples is a change in the object being verified, not the retroactive addition of missing test records to the old examples.

## Final Retained Decision

This page ultimately retains one local decision: the public statement on pagination boundaries should be recovered from the pagination result object, with the client file serving only as an entry point for old calls and code reading; theme startup should continue to be verified separately through state differences before and after calls. The old paths, old assumptions, review corrections, and two outdated examples are not deleted, because they constitute the actual sequence of this history.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Observed
    Observed --> Reviewed
    Reviewed --> OpenQuestion
```

Checks for migrating old templates initially started with event names. At the time, the usual practice was to search for terms such as `application`, `events`, `event`, `use`, and `names`, then look for related material near the file once a path was found. It provides no rules for handling domain events and does not describe the template port contract. Using it as a navigation starting point is appropriate; treating it as the event implementation location was an overreach in the early notes.

## Initial Migration Guidance

The old guidance was "leave template names unchanged and keep the old entry point in place for now." At the time, no distinction was made between names referring to events, template metadata, or caller conventions. This approach was convenient for quickly copying templates: first check whether the original name was still there, then check whether the frontend startup file could still be located. The drawback was also clear: names and paths are only surface clues and cannot answer what the application layer actually consumes.

Keeping the original name was not a mistake. It provides a shared search reference for material from before and after the migration, and avoids changing old names before call relationships have been confirmed. The problem was writing "not renaming for now" as "already compatible." What was missing between those two statements was an actual application-layer call and an independent check of the template ports.

The old process was roughly as follows:

```text
Search for event-related terms
   ↓
Find polyfills.ts
   ↓
Confirm that the zone.js import is still present
   ↓
Assume template migration can continue
```

This process is retained here, but the final step should no longer be used as a conclusion. The presence of `zone.js` confirms only one local fact at the top of the file. It does not establish the event-handling name, nor does it establish that the template port conventions still match those of the old template.

## A Marginal Note from the Review

The later review did not modify this frontend file. Instead, it first recorded the top of the file, then tried to return to the application layer to find event-related objects. There was only one marginal note: do not add event definitions to polyfills just because you see `zone.js`. This reminder addresses the problem of mistakenly modifying the entry-point file.

For migration work, the entry-point file is still useful. Maintainers can use old issue terms to find `src/Web/ClientApp/src/polyfills.ts`, confirm that they have returned to the same set of frontend material, and then continue tracing from nearby application-layer objects. Here, "continue tracing" does not mean that a complete call chain already exists; the review notes did not retain enough call examples to document a specific handler, user-facing result, or port implementation detail on that basis.

The review results should therefore be divided into three categories rather than combined into a single statement that "the template is compatible":

| Object | What could be confirmed at the time | What was still missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frontend entry point | `polyfills.ts` is an existing ts module; the top of the file imports `zone.js` | A direct relationship to event handling |
| Event name | The actual usage location in the application layer needs to be revisited | The object called, how it is called, and the result |
| template port contract | Should be checked independently | Template metadata and records of port mappings |

The gaps in the table are not conclusions of failure; they only indicate that there was no material available at the time to fill them in. This is especially true for event names: file paths and search terms can suggest a direction, but cannot replace call sites in the application layer.

## Second Walkthrough

The second walkthrough split the work into two parts. The first part handled navigation only: open `polyfills.ts`, retain the `zone.js` import and the Angular CLI comment, and confirm that the old material still points to the same frontend entry point. Only the second part addressed events: use the old name to return to the application layer, find the object that actually consumes the event, and then consider the name separately from the port conventions retained in the template.

This walkthrough did not leave enough examples to close out the second part. We did not infer an event name from the entry-point file, nor did we infer that the template ports were usable because the name had not changed. The original statement that "migration can continue as long as the name is the same" should be narrowed to: the same name can serve as a starting point for comparison, but cannot replace verification at the application layer.

The template port contract was still only an explicit checklist item at the time. It should not be appended to the `zone.js` import, nor should it automatically pass based on event-name search results. The old and current templates need to be examined using the steps maintainers normally follow; the existing notes do not list the full steps, so the unchecked parts were not marked as passed.

## Provisional Migration Approach

For now, the distinction before and after migration can be recorded as follows:

```text
Old lookup method
Old issue terms → polyfills.ts → Treat the match as the event entry point

Provisional lookup method
Old issue terms → polyfills.ts (frontend entry point)
                    ├→ Actual usage location in the application layer (pending verification)
                    └→ template port contract (pending separate verification)
```

This change does not invalidate the old path. The old path is still suitable for retrieving historical material, especially when the name has not yet been located again. The change is that the path serves only for navigation, no longer for deciding where something belongs. Restoring the old path restores the route for looking things up, not the old conclusion that "a match means the work is done."

## Items for the Next Verification

1. Find the most recent actual application-layer call associated with the old name, and record the object and how it is called.
2. Label the call site separately from `polyfills.ts` to avoid documenting proximity to frontend startup code as event-handling logic.
3. Check the template port contract using routine maintenance steps, and fill in the parts of the template metadata or port conventions that can be confirmed.
4. If there are no call examples or port records, leave the entries blank rather than using identical names to fill in a conclusion.

This is the extent of the migration notes currently available: the frontend entry point can be traced back, event naming requires returning to the application layer, and template ports must be checked separately. The old rule has not been removed, but it applies only to the first step of finding the entry point.

# Event Naming and Template Port Migration

This record originally aimed to address just one small issue: where to look up event-related names in the old template. The path recorded at the outset was later referenced repeatedly, so domain event naming, template port contract, and the frontend startup file ended up documented in the same place. These old passages are retained not because they can still directly provide a basis for judgment, but because people working on the migration will still encounter the same path first.

The migration here is not about copying a file to another directory. What needs to move is two ways of checking: event names should be traced back to where they are actually used in the application layer; the template port contract should be checked against the template's own conventions. `src/Web/ClientApp/src/polyfills.ts` remains the frontend entry point for the old material, but is not responsible for defining either of the first two items.

## The Earliest Recorded Entry Point

The old record focused on a very narrow target:

```text
internal/cleanarchitecture-core
└── src/Web/ClientApp/src/polyfills.ts
```

The following is directly visible at the top of the file:

```ts
import 'zone.js'; // Included with Angular CLI.
```

Early investigators would first search for terms such as `application`, `events`, `event`, `use`, and `names`. Once this path appeared in the results, they would continue looking around the file. This method was not without value: material for an unfamiliar template is often scattered, and a path plus a few terms from old issues can provide a repeatable starting point.

The problem at the time was that the starting point was written up as the endpoint. Placing these three facts side by side—the file exists, there are imports at the top of the file, and the search terms produce a match—can easily create the impression that "event handling is here." In fact, `polyfills.ts` only tells us that this is an existing ts module and that it includes `zone.js` from Angular CLI. It shows neither event definitions nor the template port conventions.

The old record also included this sentence: "When porting the template, keep the original names first, then handle the differences." At the time, this was merely a way to reduce the scope of changes. It did not clarify which object the original names belonged to, nor did it explain whether unchanged names meant that the callers, template metadata, and application-layer handling names would all remain unchanged. This sentence is retained as the earlier position; it is not the current basis for assessing compatibility.

## An Operational Reminder Beside the File

Someone later added a very short reminder next to the path: when you see `zone.js`, do not casually change polyfills. First record what is at the top of the file, then find where events are consumed in the application layer.

This reminder has remained useful. The most immediate mistake during migration is to treat the frontend file matched by terms from old issues as the place where event definitions need to be added. The dependencies at the top of the file are associated with frontend startup; domain event naming belongs to checks of application-layer behavior. Their proximity does not mean that one object can answer questions about the other.

Therefore, the old entry point's place in the migration should be fixed as the first step:

```text
Old issue terms
   ↓
polyfills.ts
   ↓
Verify the frontend entry point and file header
   ↓
Leave that file and trace back to the application-layer event object
```

This sequence does not guarantee that a complete call chain will be found every time. It only avoids drawing an incorrect ownership conclusion from the entry file. If tracing back stalls, record "call pending verification" rather than interpreting the import statement as event logic.

## Old approach: use names and paths to determine whether migration can continue

The complete idea behind the old approach was broader than the note beside the file. It treated migration as retaining the old template name, retaining a searchable path, and then confirming that the frontend file had not disappeared. Under this approach, the check would proceed as follows:

```text
The old template name is still visible
      ↓
Event-related terms hit polyfills.ts
      ↓
zone.js import is still present
      ↓
Assume the template is compatible and continue
```

This approach was not completely discarded because it can serve as a quick navigation aid. When someone takes over old materials, they can still use the same set of issue terms to return to the same path and confirm that they have not first wandered into an unrelated frontend location. Its limitation should also be kept in mind: names and paths can only establish an entry point for tracing back; they cannot prove which event the application layer actually handled, nor can they prove that the template port contract is aligned.

The old approach is especially unsuitable for two types of differences. The first is when the name appears unchanged but the actual usage location has not yet been found. The second is when the event name appears unchanged, but the template metadata or port conventions have not been checked. Both differences can be obscured by the judgment that "the path is still there."

## Trial run in the year 2024

The second review round attempted to break the old approach apart. The first phase still began with `src/Web/ClientApp/src/polyfills.ts`, confirming that the old entry point could be found and copying down the `zone.js` import and the Angular CLI comment from the file header. The second phase instead traced back through event-related objects in the application layer, then recorded the discovered names and the template port contract separately.

The trial run did not leave enough actual call samples. Without samples, the most that can be confirmed is that the investigation should return to the application layer; it is not possible to specify a particular call object or explain what result the user will see. This gap cannot be filled by the frontend file: the file header contains no call information, and the search terms provide no usage relationship.

A broader judgment also appeared at the time: "If the template names are the same, the migration probably will not affect callers." This was later narrowed to: "Matching names can only serve as a starting point for comparison." Consistent names can reduce some search costs, but they cannot replace confirming the actual handler name or checking the template ports.

At the time, the staging record kept the three items separate:

| Inspection target | Facts that can be retained | What should not be inferred from them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `polyfills.ts` | Existing ts module; header import `zone.js` | Ownership of the domain event implementation |
| Event-related object | Need to check back in the application layer for actual usage | The migration can be completed based solely on search hits |
| template port contract | Need to separately verify the old template against the current template | The port can be considered to have passed just because the event names are the same |

The blank cells in the table were not filled in as conclusions at the time. They indicate insufficient material, not default success. Keeping empty entries is more helpful for subsequent migration than merging two unrelated objects into a single "compatible" status.

## A verification approach that failed

A failed path was reviewed later. It was not a code execution failure; rather, the reasoning stopped midway but was still pushed forward:

```text
Search for event-related terms
      ↓
Hit src/Web/ClientApp/src/polyfills.ts
      ↓
Treat the hit path as the processing entry point
      ↓
Did not obtain the actual application-layer call
      ↓
Still tried to conclude the compatibility check using the name and file header
```

The failure occurred at the third step. `import 'zone.js'; // Included with Angular CLI.` is a clear local declaration, but it is not an event-handling relationship. Even if the file exists and the comment has not changed, the content of the template port contract cannot be filled in from there. After that review, migration records began explicitly marking the frontend entry point, application-layer event name, and template port as three adjacent but distinct objects.

This correction did not require deleting the old path. The old path can still take maintainers back to the original material. What was replaced was the purpose of the old path: previously, someone treated it as the final basis; now it is used only as a way to enter the old material.

## Retained recovery method

If a new round of checking temporarily cannot find the actual application-layer call, restore the old path first rather than guessing at the event definition in `polyfills.ts`. The recovery steps are as follows:

1. Open `src/Web/ClientApp/src/polyfills.ts` and confirm that what was found is an existing frontend entry point.
2. Record the file header's `zone.js` import to avoid mixing different frontend locations into the old record.
3. Continue locating application-layer-related objects using the old event search terms.
4. If no call sample can be found, leave the event item pending review.
5. Keep the template port contract as a separate check item; do not use the entry file or a same-name occurrence to fill in its result.

This is not a return to the old assessment. What has been restored is the lookup route, making it easier to start again from historical material. The final step in the old approach, "migration can continue as long as the path still exists," no longer applies.

The difference between the old and current approaches can be condensed into a small diagram:

```text
Old lookup method                   Current lookup method
Old issue terms                     Old issue terms
   │                                   │
   └── polyfills.ts                    ├── polyfills.ts: frontend entry point
          │                            ├── Application-layer object: event name
          └── Used as the final entry point    └── Template object: port contract
```

The diagram does not connect all engineering objects into a single chain. Here, we only need to ensure that three local relationships do not substitute for one another: the frontend path can be used for navigation, event naming belongs to the application layer, and template ports require separate confirmation.

## Traces of the division of work before review

In subsequent material, CA-204 was used to navigate domain event naming. The card recorded a caller walkthrough, indicating that the inspection had shifted from looking only at files to looking at callers. This action shows that the direction of the follow-up lookup had changed, but it did not itself provide complete call snippets or the results seen by users; a single walkthrough cannot be described as verification of all calls.

CA-204 later moved into review because the implementation had been completed on an existing branch. This progress likewise does not replace the migration record here. For this record, the cards provide entry points for follow-up lookup: when event-related calls need to be found, continue from CA-204; when template ports need to be confirmed, progress on CA-204 should not be used in place of the other check.

CA-219 is used to navigate the template port contract. After work on it began, it was blocked because the template metadata test machine was occupied by other regression testing. This blocker remains very specific: the template metadata check was not completed at that time. Therefore, template ports should not be marked as having passed merely because the frontend entry point is accessible and event names are searchable.

The two cards each serve a purpose here:

```text
CA-204 → Follow-up lookup direction for application-layer event calls
CA-219 → Inspection direction for the template port contract and template metadata
```

They are not interchangeable. The follow-up check of the event names did not fill in the template metadata; the blocked template test machine also does not invalidate the frontend entry point's continued use for navigating the legacy material. The migration record should preserve this asymmetric state.

## Current migration order

When handling the migration from old templates to 2026.09 integration train now, start by handling each object separately rather than treating a single search hit as completing all verification.

**First confirm the legacy entry.** Open `src/Web/ClientApp/src/polyfills.ts`; only confirm that it is still the existing ts module to be reviewed, and retain the `zone.js` import at the top of the file. The output of this action is a frontend entry record, not an event-handling conclusion.

**Then verify the event names.** Navigate into the application layer using the old name or CA-204, and look for the object that actually uses the event. When found, record the object or call site; when not found, the status is pending verification. Do not use `polyfills.ts`, search terms, or the template name to fill this gap.

**Verify the template port separately.** Follow CA-219 to check the template port contract. When the template metadata check is affected by the test machine being occupied, leave the item incomplete. Consistent event names cannot replace this item, and neither can the import at the top of the file.

**Finally compare against the old name.** The old name can remain as a comparison point before and after the migration. An unchanged name only indicates that no change of this kind occurred at the naming level; it does not automatically cover the verification results for application-layer calls or the template port.

Following this order, each "unconfirmed" item in the migration has a clear place: when the event call is missing, stop at the application layer; when the template metadata is missing, stop at the port check; the frontend entry point serves as navigation only in the first step. This way, even if one item is completed later than another, known and unknown states will not be conflated into a single status.

## Current application-layer requirements

After working through the earlier approach, annotations, trial runs, failure paths, and card rechecks, the current requirement is limited to application-layer event naming:

> TodoItem domain events use the Created and Completed handler names consistently across the application layer.

This requirement does not change the position of `polyfills.ts`. The frontend file remains an entry point in the legacy material and must not be written up as the place where the `TodoItem` event is handled. Nor does it provide undocumented implementation details for the template port contract; the port check must still be completed separately according to the template object.

In the migration record, the role of the application-layer requirement is to constrain where event-name verification is performed: inspect the handler names actually used in the application layer rather than guessing based on the frontend file, a search hit, or the template name. The old-version assumption that "finding the file was enough to determine compatibility" has been replaced, but the old section remains above so that it is possible to see why it once appeared reasonable.

## Issues Not Yet Removed

There is another adjacent issue that is not expanded on here: how the results obtained by tracing back application-layer calls should be included in the same migration record as the results of the template metadata checks. The existing materials do not contain enough call samples or template metadata samples, so user results, successful responses, or port details cannot be fabricated.

Another gap is the specific location of the most recent real call. The caller walkthrough in CA-204 indicates the direction but does not provide a call snippet that can be preserved verbatim. If the record is supplemented later, the priority should be to add the call target and call location rather than continuing to add search terms.

The test machine's occupied status in CA-219 should also remain part of the inspection status. Once the test machine is available again, what needs to be added is the material left by the template metadata check; the template port item cannot be closed early based on the event name or front-end path.

## Short Sentences from the Old Meeting Page

> First look at the files that can be located; do not mistake the entry point for ownership. The event name must map back to the application layer. Record template ports separately.

This short statement preserves the order of operations from that meeting. It does not provide the complete call relationships, nor does it claim that the template migration has been completed. Subsequent records only split its three objects apart and clarify at which points Fang Ke could stop.

## Appendix of Old Examples: Still Locatable, but No Longer to Be Followed

### Old Example A: End Based on the Matching Path

```text
Found polyfills.ts
Confirmed zone.js exists
Assumed the integration train could continue
```

This example is outdated. The first two steps can still be used to confirm the old entry point, but the third cannot serve as a completion signal for domain event naming or the template port contract.

### Old Example B: Infer the Same Contract from the Same Name

```text
The old template name has not changed
Therefore, the port contract does not need to be checked again
```

This example was later overturned. Consistent names only show that a comparison point remains; they cannot prove that the template metadata, application-layer handler names, and caller results have all been confirmed. This short flow is retained in the appendix, but migration should follow the current order above.

### Old Example C: Add an Explanation at the Front-End Entry Point

```text
An event-related term points to polyfills.ts
Add an event description near that file
Use the description instead of tracing back through the application layer
```

This example is no longer used either. A navigation note may be retained near the entry point, but event ownership cannot be filled in without an actual call. When restoring the old materials, first follow the path into the entry point, then return to verify the application layer and template object separately.

# Identity OpenAPI Metadata Troubleshooting Tree

When someone on the integration train reported incorrect identity OpenAPI metadata, the old procedure started at the client entry point. First, open `src/Web/ClientApp/proxy.conf.js` and look for identity-related proxy entries. The understanding at the time was that the metadata seen by the client came through this entry point, so a missing proxy entry or an incorrect target would make it look as though the definitions had not been updated.

```text
Incorrect identity OpenAPI metadata
|
+-- Reproducible through the ClientApp entry point?
|   |
|   +-- No: record the entry point first and wait for more details from the caller.
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Matching entry in proxy.conf.js?
|           |
|           +-- No: add the proxy entry and restart the client.
|           |
|           +-- Yes
|               |
|               +-- Does the proxy target match the local startup entry point?
|                   |
|                   +-- No: restore the expected target and restart.
|                   |
|                   +-- Yes: treat it as a client cache or startup-state issue.
```

At minimum, the investigation record should include: the client entry point where the issue appeared, whether a matching entry was found in the file, and whether the same content was still visible after restarting. If the record only says "OpenAPI is wrong," the next investigation will not be able to distinguish between a request bypassing the proxy, a changed proxy target, and a page still showing old results.

The judgment at the time was: if the proxy path had not changed, identity itself should not be the first suspect. That judgment applied only to reports coming through ClientApp; when the entry point is unknown, do not start by changing the OpenAPI configuration.

If the issue persisted after restarting, the old procedure was to hand the request URL to the Web side for further investigation. Without a request URL, put the investigation on hold rather than guessing an identity path.

It put nearly all identity OpenAPI metadata anomalies under the client proxy branch: first look for `src/Web/ClientApp/proxy.conf.js`, then check the identity-related items, and finally restart. This sequence was later reused, so it was not deleted outright; however, its premise is narrow—the "metadata is wrong" reported issue must in fact come from the ClientApp-related entry, and the observed change must also be traceable to a request.

The old draft did not state these premises. It connected "someone saw an anomaly on the client," "there are adjacent proxy entries in the file," and "the screen changed after a restart" into a single causal chain. All three can be true at the same time without constituting proof of one another. The later note was not intended to create a new, comprehensive explanation of identity OpenAPI metadata, but to record the stopping points that the old tree would skip beside the existing entry.

First, the part that remains usable. When a report contains only the issue name, with no screenshot, request location, or explanation of which entry produced the conclusion, `proxy.conf.js` is a specific local inspection point. The old procedure interpreted "not found" as "the rule is missing" and then recommended adding the item. This interpretation remains in the historical tree because that is how early tickets were handled; the later note no longer treats it as an automatic recovery action. A rule not being found may mean that the lookup path is incorrect, or it may mean that this entry does not pass through that configuration in the first place. The current material does not provide a complete call relationship, so a blank cannot be used to replace it with the conclusion that configuration is missing.

## The Old Tree's Original Flow

Below is the branch organized according to the old guidance. The actions in the tree describe where they directed people at the time; they do not mean that these actions are sufficient to determine the source of the metadata.

```text
Observed an anomaly in identity OpenAPI metadata
|
+-- Did the report come from ClientApp?
|   |
|   +-- Unknown
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Old handling: start by treating it as a client entry point issue and open proxy.conf.js.
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Found a proxy entry adjacent to identity?
|           |
|           +-- No
|           |   |
|           |   +-- Old handling: add the proxy entry and restart the client.
|           |
|           +-- Yes
|               |
|               +-- Does the target appear to match the startup entry point?
|                   |
|                   +-- No: Old handling: change the target, then restart.
|                   |
|                   +-- Yes
|                       |
|                       +-- Did the anomaly disappear after restarting?
|                           |
|                           +-- Yes: Old handling: record it as proxy caching.
|                           |
|                           +-- No: Old handling: record it as startup state and hand it over to the Web side.
|
+-- Did the report not come from ClientApp, or is that unconfirmed?
    |
    +-- Old handling: still prioritize checking the client configuration.
```

The last box is the most misleading part of this record. The old tree treated an unconfirmed entry point as "there is no harm in checking the proxy first." In practice, this leads to a series of trial changes: first add an entry, then adjust the target, then use the page after restarting as the result. Even if the screen changes, no evidence is retained to show which step had an effect. The old tree did not record this gap, so it looks like a short, smooth recovery path.

This version does not remove the old tree or repackage it as the current workflow. Old tickets may still refer to its terms: proxy entry, target, cache, startup state. When reading these tickets, keep in mind that these terms were mostly handling labels used at the time, not necessarily verified causes.

## First, write down where you saw it

identity OpenAPI metadata was treated as a single term in the early records. Some people used it to refer to the definition content on the page, while others may simply have meant that identity-related information still looked outdated. The old draft did not require reporters to distinguish between these descriptions, so as soon as "the metadata is wrong" appeared, troubleshooting jumped straight to the proxy file.

The first step added in the supplementary notes is small: first record where the anomaly appeared. This can be written as the client entry point, the request result location, or not yet determined. There is no requirement here to expand the observation into a full list of fields; it only needs to tell the person taking over where the problem was first seen.

If the location has not yet been determined, stop at the original description. Do not translate "outdated," "missing," or "inconsistent" into specific OpenAPI items, or into a client proxy anomaly. The old draft would continue at this point because it assumed that every report came from ClientApp; this assumption was part of the old approach.

If the location is clearly an entry point related to ClientApp, then record whether a request path is available from the same observation. Without a path, you can still check `proxy.conf.js`, but the result of that check can only be recorded as "an adjacent rule exists" or "no adjacent rule found." Do not write "the request went through the proxy" or "the proxy did not match" on that basis. Whether a rule exists and whether a request passed through it are two different facts.

The record format was later condensed to a few lines, not to make every troubleshooting session a long write-up:

```text
Location of occurrence:
Observed behavior:
Request path:
proxy.conf.js:
After restart:
```

If any of these items was not obtained, write "not obtained" or leave it blank. Do not use "same as above" in place of the entry point and path after restart; if the page or the way it was accessed changed after restart, what was seen may no longer be the same phenomenon. In the May version, "normal after restart" was often written up as a conclusion about caching, but that line usually did not preserve the conditions for the before-and-after comparison.

## Pause at the file

`src/Web/ClientApp/proxy.conf.js` is the path given in the old troubleshooting records. It is suitable for local navigation, but cannot by itself determine where identity OpenAPI metadata belongs. If adjacent identity-related rules can be found in the file, first record the path prefix in the rule separately from the request path seen during the investigation. Do not just write "matches."

When both the path prefix and the request path contained the word identity, the old approach tended to treat them as the same object. This simplification helped with quick identification, but obscured differences in scope: one is a prefix visible in the configuration, and the other is a request observed on a particular occasion. Without recording both individually, people following up cannot know whether the supposed "match" means a complete correspondence, prefix coverage, or merely similar names.

If only the page location can be obtained, but not the path, file inspection can still continue, but it should not trigger configuration changes. The old draft recommended "add it if it cannot be found", because the proxy entry was considered a prerequisite for client metadata at the time. The addendum retains this historical recommendation while adding a stopping point: do not add rules until it has been confirmed that the request will reach this configuration.

If the path can be obtained, but the corresponding entry is not found in the file, the record should clearly state "path obtained, rule not found". This is slower than writing "proxy missing", and also less likely to misrepresent the lookup target as a configuration defect. This section does not require the on-duty team to trace the issue all the way to other implementation locations; this page covers only the local entry point of client configuration, and relationships beyond it need to be checked further against actual references.

If the path and adjacent rules appear to match, do not immediately change the proxy target either. First record the target as a configuration fact, then record the entry point and behavior observed this time. A target that appears different from the local startup entry point does not automatically mean it caused the metadata change. The old procedure would directly write the target back, then judge whether recovery had occurred based on whether the page refreshed; the old records did not consistently retain before-and-after results for the same request, so this step is difficult to review retrospectively.

The stopping point here can easily be misread as "do nothing". That is not the intent. Inspecting the file, recording the path, identifying the entry point, and returning to the same screen are all valid actions. What is being stopped is directly elevating these local observations into "identity itself has no problem" or "the proxy configuration is the cause".

## Why the restart box remains

Restarting the client was the most frequently used recovery action in the old document. It has not been erased from the historical record, because some early descriptions left only "it worked after restarting". Removing this step would lead later readers to mistakenly believe that no action had been taken at the time; presenting it as a definite fix would repeat the old misjudgment.

A restart can be used to observe again, but it may change more than one thing at once: the page state starts over, the client process restarts, and the order in which entry points are accessed may also differ. Without records of the entry points, paths, and visible content before and after, the most accurate conclusion is only "not seen again after restarting" or "still seen after restarting".

"Proxy cache" in the old tree is not a verified endpoint. It was the term used at the time for "no longer appeared after restarting". Similarly, "startup state" was the term for "the anomaly persisted after restarting". The two labels helped with classification in the old tickets, but should not replace what was actually observed.

The results of observing again can be saved using the following two lines:

```text
Before restart: entry point / path / displayed content
After restart: entry point / path / displayed content
```

If only one half is available, do not fill in the other half. In particular, do not write "cache cleared" just because the entry point changed after restarting and the anomaly was temporarily not seen. Recovery narratives in the old draft often ended here, so they did not leave behind the boundaries of the issue that could be assessed later.

When the issue still appeared after restarting, the old procedure would hand it off to the Web team. This action can be retained, but the handoff material should not consist only of "metadata is still incorrect". At a minimum, include the initial location where it appeared, the path obtained, the adjacent rules seen in `proxy.conf.js`, and whether the before-and-after observations used the same entry point. If these items are not yet available, the handoff note should explicitly retain the gaps rather than replace them with "proxy is normal".

## Two very similar reports that should not be merged

During the integration train, identity OpenAPI metadata and exception response metadata can easily appear together in a single report. Both contain the text OpenAPI, but that does not mean they represent the same exception, nor does it mean that the results from one branch can validate the other branch.

The old draft did not separate these two objects. As a result, descriptions related to exception responses were sometimes placed in the proxy tree, or a change in the identity information on the page was taken to mean that the exception response had recovered. This habit remains in the wording of older issues, but it is no longer suitable as a basis for assessment.

If both phenomena are indeed mentioned in the field, first record the original observations separately. Continue to record the identity side by entry point, path, and client configuration; retain the material for exception response metadata separately in DOC-20. If both sides lack an entry point, stop each one separately as well. Do not use page changes on one side to fill in the cause on the other.

This does not require completing the investigation of both sets of material every time. When a report only involves identity OpenAPI metadata, there is no need to introduce exception responses for completeness; when a report only contains exception responses, do not first rewrite it as an identity proxy issue either. The flaw in the old troubleshooting records was not that they used a short filename as an entry point, but that they mistook adjacent names for identical handling paths.

## Deprecated quick-recovery claims

Three phrases appeared repeatedly in early tickets: add a proxy entry, change the proxy target, and restart the client. At the time, they were linked into a short chain of "exception—change configuration—recovery". These phrases can still be found today; the following only adds the conditions under which they apply, without erasing the historical actions.

**Add a proxy entry.** The old advice was to add it if it could not be found. The narrower conditions for using this approach are: the observation is already known to come from ClientApp, the request path has already been obtained, and the existing rules have been confirmed not to cover that path. Without the first two conditions, "cannot be found" may still simply mean that the right location has not been checked. The May version did not require these conditions, so it automatically interpreted blank areas in the file as missing configuration.

**Change the proxy target.** The old advice was to change the target back if it looked wrong. Comparing the target with the local startup entry point can only show that there is a configuration difference; it cannot, on its own, explain where identity OpenAPI metadata comes from, nor can it explain what the change will affect. If a change is indeed made, the record should separate the change from the page observations. Do not write "metadata has recovered" to mean "the target was changed".

**Restart the client.** The old advice was that if it disappeared after a restart, it was a cache issue. Disappearance after a restart only means that the next observation did not show the same phenomenon; persistence after a restart only means that the next observation still showed an anomaly. Both outcomes require returning to the location where it appeared and the path; neither can serve as a cause label on its own.

These limitations are not an alternative recovery procedure established later. The available material does not provide a complete path for generating identity metadata, nor does it provide commands or examples applicable to all startup methods. Adding common operations would make this old document look more complete, but it would turn environments that never appeared in the record into established facts.

## October Addendum

CA-208 later went through security triage and moved from To Do to In Progress. This means the entry point for checking identity OpenAPI metadata was reopened; it does not mean any conclusion has been reached about the relationships among proxy entries, client pages, and metadata. Early records tended to describe similar status changes as "a fix has already started"; that wording was not used this time.

At the time of this addendum, `src/Web/ClientApp/proxy.conf.js` was still retained as an entry point that could be opened. The reason is simple: both the old issue name and the call name point here, so investigators do not have to start looking for files from scratch. But this navigation only supports inspecting local relationships in the current revision; it cannot elevate a configuration path into implementation ownership. If further confirmation is needed about whether a request passed through a rule, use the references actually observed during that reproduction.

When reviewing the old handling, the most obvious gap was inconsistent record granularity. Some tickets recorded only the client entry point, some only the filename, and some only the screen after a restart. None of them can independently answer why identity OpenAPI metadata changed, yet they can be stitched together into a seemingly complete story in later summaries. The purpose of this addendum is only to prevent that stitching: entry points, paths, rules, and restart results are recorded separately, and unknowns are not filled in using neighboring words.

This document still carries the old judgment: in ClientApp reports, look at the proxy file first. That judgment has not been rewritten as "all anomalies start on the generation side," nor has it been declared completely invalid. It simply can no longer carry any additional implications. Specifically, looking at the file first can help confirm whether the old configuration exists; seeing a rule does not prove that the current request passed through it; seeing a change after a restart does not prove proxy caching; without an entry point and a path, a metadata issue cannot be closed out as a configuration change.

## The Shortest Record to Keep While On Call

When time is tight, there is no need to complete every box in the entire tree. Keeping four to five lines is already more useful than old tickets that recorded only the issue name:

```text
Location:
Behavior:
Path:
proxy.conf.js:
After restart:
```

For "Location," record where the observation occurred, not a presumed component name. For "Behavior," preserve the other person's original wording; if all that is known is "old," write "old," and do not independently expand it into a description, field, or response content. For "Path," write "not obtained" if none is available. For "proxy.conf.js," record the adjacent rule found, or "not found," rather than "proxy confirmed." For "After restart," describe only the next observation, and also record any change in the entry point.

If the location is unclear, stop at the first line and wait for entry-point information. If the location is clear but there is no path, you can check the configuration file, then stop at observing the rules. If no relationship has been established between the path and the rules, record the discrepancy; do not add rules to fill the gap. If it no longer appears after a restart, write that it did not appear again; do not classify it as a cache issue. If it still appears after a restart, continue the handoff with the material already available; do not treat "startup state" as a conclusion.

This shorthand is not entirely consistent with the quick recovery procedure from May. It retains the entry point to the old file, but refuses to add evidence to support the old conclusions. For records that have already cited the old tree, this inconsistency is necessary: the old draft explains why the proxy was changed first at the time; the addendum explains why those changes cannot automatically explain the source of identity OpenAPI metadata.

## Parts not yet filled in

- The old records did not establish a consistent account of whether identity OpenAPI metadata at different client entry points refers to the same observed object.
- The relationship between adjacent rules in `proxy.conf.js` and an actual request needs to be confirmed in a specific reproduction.
- If the same entry point and path are not available from before and after the restart, the historical "cache" classification cannot be retrospectively verified.
- If a specific entry point is added to CA-208, bring the entry-point and path material back here, rather than leaving only a card status change.

Therefore, this page is still not suitable for use as the current complete recovery manual. It preserves a client-proxy-first path that once circulated, along with the pause points later added to that path. For reports that contain only the issue name, you can start by inspecting the file; for reports missing an entry point or path, do not continue to substitute adding proxy entries, changing the target, or restarting for facts.

# Exception Response Metadata Migration Notes

This record still starts from the old investigation path. After exception response metadata was placed on the compatibility review list for the 2026.09 integration train, the old materials led readers to `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/web-api-client.ts` by issue name and call name. This entry has not been removed: it explains why the React client was examined at the time and gives legacy links a place that can still be revisited.

But the entry itself does not explain where the metadata is generated, where it is attached, or which usage point needs to be migrated. Early notes wrote the filename directly as the migration target, and later tried to explain it using the import in the file header. Both forms should be kept because they reflect how the search was conducted at the time; they must no longer be organized into a current workflow that only appears to have been confirmed.

The wording on the old page about "starting changes from the client file" is now historical context only. It helps people understand the scope of the old review, but it is no longer an operation instruction. After finding the file, first distinguish which question this round is meant to answer: is it reconstructing the usage point corresponding to the old issue, or confirming whether a usage point contains information related to exception responses? The two questions may produce different sets of references. They cannot be recorded as the same set of migration targets merely because both start from the same file.

## The Old Entry That Remains

The issue name, call name, and file location used by the old record should be carried over together. If only the path is kept, it will eventually be unclear why this module was opened in the first place; if only the issue name is kept, it will be difficult to return to the actual location examined at the time. The value of the old path is locating the material, not attributing responsibility.

`web-api-client.ts` is treated in this record as an existing TypeScript module. It was once the starting point for code reading and historical behavior review. The old record points from the issue name and call name to this location, which supports, at most, "this is worth opening first"; it does not support "the exception response is definitely handled here." The previous wording compressed these two meanings into one sentence, making it sound as though responsibility for handling had already been settled. That impression should be withdrawn.

The old entry has another aspect that can easily cause misinterpretation. After seeing the filename, someone may casually include nearby objects in the same file in scope; that approach is suitable for temporary browsing, but not for leaving a migration record. The fact that exception response metadata and an adjacent module appear in the same reading view does not mean that they have an implementation relationship. The old notes do not record results sufficient to connect them, so this page does not add that relationship.

## The Clue in the File Header

The direct dependency visible in the file header is as follows:

```ts
import followIfLoginRedirect from './components/api-authorization/followIfLoginRedirect';
```

This import is currently the only explicitly recorded adjacency within the file. It shows that when reading `web-api-client.ts`, `followIfLoginRedirect` is a visible adjacent object; it does not show that the redirect helper constructs exception response metadata, nor that an exception response must pass through that helper.

Earlier records treated this import as the "next stop." This order is not entirely useless: when a module reference does not lead to a suitable location, opening the helper can rule out an obvious adjacent direction. The problem is that it too easily steers the record toward login redirects, so later readers may interpret "was once examined" as "has been confirmed relevant." Therefore, this old recommendation is retained but downgraded to a conditional branch.

```text
The retained old entry
Issue name / call name
        |
        v
web-api-client.ts

Current verification order
web-api-client.ts --find references--> Usage-point record
        |
        `--view if necessary--> followIfLoginRedirect
```

The lines in the diagram indicate reading order only, not a runtime call graph. The condition for the branch on the right is that references to `web-api-client.ts` have already been checked, the old issue name still cannot be mapped to a verifiable usage point, and the current review genuinely needs to rule out the influence of the file-header adjacency. If the goal is merely to complete a full path, do not enter the helper.

After viewing the helper, the record can stop at "connection observed," "no connection observed," or "not yet determined." When there is no connection, return to the file references rather than using a login redirect as a substitute for an explanation of the exception response. When the matter is not yet determined, it should not be added to the migration scope merely because the import exists. The most error-prone part of the old notes was not viewing the helper, but prematurely writing the viewing action as a conclusion.

## Order for Moving the Record Out of the Old Path

First, retain the old issue name and call name. Do not rush to replace them with a new module description. The old terms may not be precise enough, but they are why the old material led to this file; after they are removed, later readers will see only a client path and will not be able to tell how it relates to this round of compatibility review.

Second, fix `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/web-api-client.ts` in place and note that the search is directed at `v_prev`. This step handles historical location, not code ownership. Later directory or implementation changes should not retroactively rewrite the file entry used at the time.

Third, extract only the local facts already exposed by the file: it is a TypeScript module and directly imports `followIfLoginRedirect`. These two points are enough for the next review to start from the same location. Do not expand them in the migration notes into a client error-handling diagram, and do not infer the production location of exception response metadata from the import.

Only the fourth step is to search for references to the module. Each result worth retaining must be checked against the old issue name once. When it matches, record why it is a usage point pending review; when it does not, record it as an adjacent reference that has already been examined, without borrowing the theme of exception response metadata. This is somewhat slower than the old record, but it prevents other uses of the same file from being mistaken for part of this round's compatibility scope.

Reference results can currently be recorded in three ways. When a usage point matching the old issue is found, the file remains the entry point, while the usage point becomes the object for subsequent review. When a reference is found but its connection to the exception response is unclear, retain the fact that it is an adjacent use and do not include it in the migration. When no usable reference is obtained, stop the record at "entered the file from the old record"; do not expand the scope of responsibility just because there is an import in the file header.

This is not an acceptance classification, nor does it require the first result every time. It only ensures that the old issue name is not lost during reorganization and that anyone reviewing the record knows at which action it stopped. The earlier order of "check the import first, then find the caller" may still serve as a personal browsing habit when time is limited, but it must not replace searching for references to `web-api-client.ts`.

## Batches and Restoring the Old Path

Here, batches refer to the order in which the verification record is organized, not code release batches. The first batch only carries over the old issue name, call name, file path, and revision; it does not determine implementation responsibility. The second batch handles module references, separating usage points that match the old issue from references that are merely adjacent. Only the third batch allows `followIfLoginRedirect` to be viewed, and that happens only when the second batch does not provide a usable location.

This batching comes from rolling back an earlier judgment. Previous notes described `web-api-client.ts` as the handling point, so later readers would skip reference searches as soon as they saw the file. The only facts that can be retained with confidence are that the file can serve as a reading entry and that it has one direct import. Therefore, the wording "the file is the handling point" is withdrawn, and the record is restored to two parts: the old entry and reference verification. No code change is being reverted here; what is being reverted is the note-taking practice of writing navigation as attribution.

If a new round of searching produces no reference result that can be retained, restoring the path does not mean deleting this page or switching to another speculative module. Keep the combination of the old issue name and `web-api-client.ts`, and note that this round was not expanded; the next round should still start from this combination. If the helper branch has already been examined but produced no connection related to the exception response, retain that observation as well, so the same import is not later treated as a new discovery.

The old process has not been completely erased. The shortcut of reading the import first remains on this page so that people can understand what was previously checked; it is no longer suitable as the default migration order. The old path is useful, but the old method of attributing responsibility is no longer applicable. Both judgments should be retained.

## Boundary with Adjacent Records

problem-details handling is documented separately in DOC-21. The two pages can link to each other, but they should not be merged into one migration chain without a connection result. DOC-21 retain their own test targets; this page retains the historical entry, file adjacency, and reference verification for exception response metadata. Putting the two topics in the same paragraph would cause "both belong to error responses" to be misread as "they have the same implementation location."

This page also does not provide an assignee for the usage point. A filename, an old call name, and one import are insufficient to determine which side should handle it; only after a reference result reaches a specific object is there a basis for continuing the assessment. This blank remains because the previous mistake was precisely treating the entry as the responsibility location too early.

Still to be added is the reference review for `web-api-client.ts` in `v_prev`, along with a usage point that genuinely matches the old issue name. Until that is complete, the old path can still serve review and follow-up, but it should not be read as the current implementation map for exception response metadata.
