# Web Startup Registration Decision Record

The draft left behind not a conclusion about a startup implementation, but a choice about how to handle an old record: the term web startup registration remains, with `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/serviceWorkerRegistration.js` placed beside it. The two are not interchangeable. The former is the topic people used for searching in this integration train, while the latter is the openable JavaScript module.

After this review, the original choice remains unchanged, but the problem it addresses needs to be stated more clearly. The path is no longer merely a filename in a note; it is the first code object to check when following up on this topic. Accordingly, this record does not elevate the path into the sole location of startup registration, nor does it describe the path as the owner of client startup behavior. The decision remains: retain the path as the follow-up entry point; descriptions of the actual relationship must follow references that can be confirmed.

## Three approaches compared in the draft

The first approach treated `serviceWorkerRegistration.js` as the fixed ownership location for web startup registration. It had one obvious advantage: after entering through the issue name, readers did not first have to explain why this file should be opened. Similar records could also directly reuse the same object, making the material appear well concentrated.

The cost of this advantage was compressing judgments at different levels into a single sentence. A file path can answer "Where should I look first?"; local declarations can answer "What direct content does this module contain?"; adjacent navigation can help continue reading; only reference relationships may answer "Who uses it?" and how that use relates to a particular startup flow. The original material did not spell out the latter two levels of relationship. Registering the path as implementation ownership would make later readers think those relationships had already been confirmed earlier.

The second approach recorded only web startup registration and left out the file. This avoided prematurely specifying a module, but it also gave maintainers no concrete place to start. Each time a similar entry appeared, they would have to start searching again from the broad Web directory; people working from the same issue name might stop at different objects, and the historical records would lose comparability.

The third approach was the one actually adopted in the draft: retain the file and the issue name together, use the file for location, and stop the relationship judgment at what the existing material can support. It did not claim that the module does not participate in startup, nor did it claim that the module necessarily participates. This narrower decision may look conservative, but it preserves two things that already have value: the module lead left by the old investigation, and the room to correct the old judgment later using actual references.

The third approach continues to be used after review. The reason is not to establish uniform wording for every Web startup issue, but that this record has always had only one subject: how the old material uses this specific module location.

## What this review added

This round confirms that the path corresponds to the existing JavaScript module in the React client, making it suitable for code reading and historical behavior checks. This confirmation is sufficient to continue writing the full path in maintenance material, and sufficient to start reading from the module's local declarations. It does not make "startup registration is handled by this module" a conclusion that can be written.

The previous gap was not the absence of a filename, but that the filename was easily read as having different meanings in different records. Sometimes it was merely the entry point where an old investigation moved from the issue name and call name into the code; sometimes readers understood it as the endpoint of the complete execution chain; and some, because no call relationship had yet been obtained, instead believed that the path itself should not be retained. Neither of the latter two interpretations is appropriate. The former goes beyond the material, while the latter discards confirmed location information.

The review therefore added only one usage rule: the module location may be written first, and the specific relationship later. If a code reading session sees only local declarations, the record should stop at the local declarations; if clear references are found through adjacent navigation, then add the referenced object and the relationship that can be confirmed to that record. Do not infer execution order, loading time, or responsibility boundaries merely because a filename resembles the topic.

Here, "adjacent navigation" means the direction of reading that continues from around the module to look for references and related objects; it is not an already confirmed call graph. Its purpose is to make it unnecessary to restart the check from the entire client directory. If readers stop at this level, they can still accurately say that they found the module location; they must not package the stopping point as a complete startup description.

## Boundaries of the decisions made

Decision one: `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/serviceWorkerRegistration.js` remains the first follow-up entry point for web startup registration. When a new note, task description, or code-reading record needs to point to this topic, it may use this path to bring readers back to the same local object.

Decision two: the path name, directory location, and keywords from the old investigation are not used to assign implementation ownership. They are location clues, not proof of runtime relationships. If a reference is confirmed later, write only the scope actually supported by that reference; do not use it to define the entire Web startup process.

Decision three: the historical record will not delete the retained judgment from the draft. The draft did not have sufficient relationship material at the time, and that fact should be preserved. If it is later found that the registration relationship indicated by the topic is elsewhere, the old path remains the follow-up clue from that time; what needs correction is the overly strong interpretation, not the removal of the old clue from the history.

Decision four: when a broader client startup description is needed, establish the material separately through relationships among multiple actual objects. Do not expand this page into a directory overview and then pack unconfirmed modules, configurations, or startup stages into the description of the same path. DOC-23 may serve as navigation to adjacent material in the same integration train, but the interface review concerning Aspire resource naming in that material must not be used to infer this Web module's relationship.

Together, these decisions constrain the recording method, not the module's runtime semantics. They keep the old issue name searchable, keep the file openable, and allow later findings to be added to the existing material rather than overturning an entire vague statement.

## Rejected wording and its consequences

Using "service worker registration is Web's startup registration" as shorthand was once considered. It is convenient to read and can also connect the topic and filename in one sentence, but the existing material establishes only a search clue between the two. The name of `serviceWorkerRegistration.js` being similar to the registration in the issue name does not mean that the two already constitute interchangeable technical definitions. This shorthand is not adopted.

It was also considered to put the file path only in a temporary task and not preserve the judgment in the long-term record. This would save a page of maintenance text, but later readers would see only the task topic and would not know why this file was chosen or why it was not directly categorized as the startup implementation. The actual value left by the draft is this tradeoff, not a single line containing a path, so the decision record is retained.

Another rejected direction was to first assume that it belonged to the startup boundary and revise it only if a counterexample appeared. This direction appears to improve recording efficiency, but in practice it shifts the correction cost to later readers. Finding a reference later does not mean that the early ownership judgment was correct; it may only show that the module is connected to a particular local object. Writing a strong conclusion first would force later material to spend considerable space explaining why it had to be withdrawn, whereas the draft's narrower wording does not require this kind of remediation.

The opposite conservative approach was also discussed: because there was no complete call relationship, do not place any module location alongside the topic. This is also not adopted. The path is the part of the existing material that can be checked reliably. Deleting it would not increase accuracy; it would only leave subsequent checks without a starting point. What is retained here is a differentiated clue, not an unverified implementation assertion.

## Relationship to the task record

CA-211 is used to navigate this gap-filling work. The card later recorded a capacity review and the action of starting work, indicating that this gap entered the maintenance process. These do not change the technical judgment on this page: task status cannot show who references the module, nor can it replace reading the local declarations and adjacent objects.

Therefore, if the task record only needs to state the processing location, it can point to this page and the module path; if it needs to state a specific call relationship, the object and evidence should be written separately after the relationship has been read. Putting both types of information together is more convenient, but their meanings differ. The former answers where to start looking; only the latter may explain why a particular use is related to the startup process.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Topic: web startup registration
    Topic --> Module: Open serviceWorkerRegistration.js
    Module --> LocalRead: Read local declarations
    LocalRead --> ReferenceCheck: Continue checking references
    ReferenceCheck --> RelationRecorded: Confirmed local relationship
    ReferenceCheck --> Pending: No reference obtained
    Pending --> Module: Follow-up review
```

The diagram does not connect the module directly to "startup implementation." This is an intentionally preserved gap. The topic can lead to the module, and the module can lead to reference checking; only after a specific relationship is obtained does it enter the relationship record. When no reference is obtained, return to the module; do not fill in a seemingly complete endpoint based on the path name.

## How to add follow-up notes

If a clear reference is found in a later record, write the referenced object first, followed by the actual relationship that can be confirmed between it and the module. If it can only be confirmed that the module still exists, that the local declarations are still readable, or that adjacent navigation still points to the same scope, there is no need to attach a generalized startup explanation. Keeping local findings local in expression instead makes it easier for the next review to see what is still missing.

If future reading shows that the registration mentioned in the old investigation points to another object, retain the original decision here and append a correction: explain which relationship issue the new object addresses and whether the old path still serves the location function it had at the time. Do not merge the two objects into one vague "startup registration location." That would both lose the historical judgment and leave the new evidence without a clear place to land.

What remains unconfirmed is whether the existing references can connect the module to a specific startup location, and whether separate client startup material covering multiple objects needs to be created. Until these questions have direct object relationships, this record will continue to retain only the path, the tradeoffs, and the recheck method.

# Aspire Resource Naming Trial Proposal

This proposal was initially left in place because, during the interface review, someone put the Aspire resource naming issue and the server-side Angular module on the same investigation path. The page continued to be referenced later not because it had already defined the naming rules, but because that investigation path had not been split apart in time. The old link stops at `src/Web/ClientApp/src/app/app.server.module.ts`, so this record is being kept for now.

The initial working assumptions remain unchanged:

> If the resource name needs to follow server module assembly, `app.server.module.ts` could be the place to put the name; otherwise, keep a separate naming record and avoid turning both AppModule and AppComponent into name carriers.

The useful part of this judgment at the time was that it split "where the name is changed" from "whether the call can be traced back here" into two steps. Its problem is also clear: the entry point was inferred from the issue name and call name, not from a verified resource definition. The initial draft recorded neither the name text, the call location, nor the result seen by the user, so it cannot be used to decide the prefix, casing, or separator, much less to designate the server module as the naming owner.

## Boundaries left after review

What can be seen directly this time is a set of adjacent modules at the head of this file:

```ts
import { NgModule } from '@angular/core';
import { ServerModule } from '@angular/platform-server';
import { AppComponent } from './app.component';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
```

This content shows the Angular server module, root component, and application module organized in the same place; the visible excerpt provides neither an Aspire resource name nor how the name is passed to the caller. The initial draft treated `ServerModule` as a possible naming boundary. That was a convenient guess for continuing the search, not a confirmed design.

The guess is not being rewritten here. The old investigation relied on it, and readers entering the file through the old link can still understand why it stopped here. From the perspective of the current review, however, it can only serve as a candidate entry point: if the call chain really does pass through this module, reassess it; if the call chain has already determined the name before entering this file, do not add a mapping here just to accommodate the old conclusion.

## Trial for this round

CA-212 is the current verification entry point. The card description asks us to locate the actual call behind the most recent report of Aspire resource naming and restore how it was called and what the user saw. The proposal does not fabricate that call for the card; first, limit the material to be compared to records of the same name in three places: the object that initiated the call, the place where the name was passed or decided, and the text the user actually saw.

Once a sample is available, assess it in this order:

1. First, write down the exact name used by the call; do not normalize it into a new alias.
2. As the call enters `app.server.module.ts`, record only whether it actually passes through that module; passing through it does not automatically mean the name was generated there.
3. If the name was fixed before this point, retain the separate-record approach and stop pursuing the old server-module location.
4. If the name is selected or replaced here, compare the impact on existing calls of keeping the mapping close to the module versus keeping an external record.

"Separate record" here refers only to a storage approach in the trial; it does not mean that a new configuration file or unified naming table already exists. Its purpose is to avoid treating the resource name and the Angular module reference as the same thing when there is no call sample.

## Candidate directions

**Keep the name close to the server module.** The benefit is a short path from the old investigation, so readers opening the area around this file can see the assembly relationship. The cost is that if the name is actually determined by an earlier call, this creates a second, easily misleading entry point. Keep this direction only if the sample shows that the name is in fact selected, replaced, or bound here.

**Keep the naming record outside the module.** The benefit is that references to `NgModule`, `ServerModule`, `AppComponent`, and `AppModule` will not be interpreted as a resource declaration. The cost is that readers must continue from the call sample and cannot locate it using only the old path. The current review is closer to this direction, but there is still not enough material to elevate it to a decision.

**Defer the naming approach.** Do not change where the name lives; keep the old assumption alongside the sample still to be checked. This will not resolve the naming question from the review, but it avoids adding migration cost for an unverified location. This round adopts this direction until CA-212 is supplemented with a call that can be reviewed.

## Retraction and open items

If the call that is added does not enter `app.server.module.ts`, retract the premise that the server module is the naming boundary, and retain the old link only as a historical lead. If the call enters this file but the name has already been fixed, also retract the plan to place the mapping here. Reopen the first candidate direction only if the name is selected or transformed at that module.

Still undecided:

- Which object provides the resource name first;
- Whether the old name still appears in the caller's interface;
- Whether a name change requires compatibility with existing calls;
- After the sample is found, whether this old path should still be kept as navigation.

This page can therefore explain why that review started with the server module, but it should not be treated as the current guidance for Aspire resource naming.

# Web Integration Exit Window Checklist

This checklist originally focused only on the exit action and the last screen left on the page. After the window ends, adj-web still treats these two items as handoff criteria: the exit action must have an actual handoff entry point, and the last page display must be viewable alongside the current revision at that time. This page does not sign off on whether the release succeeded.

The old version said, "If the page has no new errors and the last screen is still there, treat the exit as complete." This judgment was not removed. It fit the practice at the time of capturing only the live state, and it also left several later unresolved states outside the window.

## When Opening the Window

- [ ] Access the current entry point once; do not substitute summary text for the actual page. Retain the original input, current revision, and first visible result.
- [ ] Record the exit action to be performed this time and who will take over when it is complete. Groups that have been taken offline should no longer be included in the new entry; follow the routing confirmation in CAA-014 for the handoff path.
- [ ] Separate the source artifact for the current entry from corroborating evidence in other pages and logs. The follow-up-check requirements in CAA-009 preserve this distinction; do not treat display text as the source artifact.
- [ ] If temporary permissions or bypasses have been borrowed, first record where they will be removed. An action without a removal location does not enter this window.

Here, "current entry point" means the entry point the caller actually opened for this call, not a similarly named page. Being able to open the entry point only shows that the page is accessible; the old checklist still treated that as the same criterion as exit completion.

## Executing the Exit Action

1. With the entry point left unchanged, perform the exit action once. Do not patch the adapter while executing it; the changed page and the original input can no longer be compared side by side.
2. When the page has a final display, retain it along with the exit action's status. The old rule treats this as the primary basis for completion, even if the page provides no new confirmation text.
3. Remove the temporary permissions and bypasses used for this run. If removal would cross the current interface, stop immediately; leave anything not removed in the handoff record, and do not use this checklist to expand the scope further.
4. Before cleaning up the routes for the old exit action, retain a snapshot of the routes before the change. CAA-017 records remnants of the old routes; do not erase the pre-change destinations just to close the window.

The implicit premise of step 3 in the old version was that, if the page's last display was still visible, the caller had already exited. This premise did not require another request to be made, nor did it require comparing the page display with later results item by item. The checklist therefore gave more weight to retaining a sample than to confirming the result.

## Window Closure Record

Before closing the window, leave at least these two items:

- [ ] Whether the exit action has been executed, and what the last visible result was.
- [ ] For each temporary permission, bypass, and old route, whether it was removed, not removed, or outside this window.

Do not use "the project team will continue to monitor" in place of a handoff record. Exit actions not completed in the window must point to an actual handoff entry point; the release decision is still confirmed separately by the corresponding owner. Adaptation outside the entry point, subsequent changes by the caller, and handling by the core project are not included here.

The early checklist allowed the window to close once the page display had been retained, and triggered recovery only on "the entry point cannot be opened": when the entry point cannot be opened, restore the pre-change route snapshot and revert this bypass; when the entry point can still be opened, do not continue cleaning up. This is the old handling retained on this page.

## Later Follow-Up

The review records in CAA-004 showed another state: the exit entry point could be opened, but the current result kept spinning. It was not caught by the old "entry point cannot be opened" branch; under the old rule, if the entry point could be opened and the last screen was still there, the window could still be considered ready to close.

The same round of follow-up did not split the spinning state into two confirmable cases. The investigation in CAA-001 ultimately ended because the existing samples could not distinguish between the two cases. Therefore, this draft has not rewritten the spinning state as a new failure criterion, nor has it added a new set of release conditions. When the page continues spinning, retain the original input and the display from that time; do not backfill a zero result; if the exit action has not yet been executed, stop before the action.

This is why this checklist is not suitable as the basis for a release: it can capture the exit state, but it does not prove that the caller obtained a stable result. The old version still treats "the last screen is visible" as sufficient; later records only show that this condition encountered a boundary, and it was not replaced within this page.

## Review Alongside the Page During Handoff

The maintenance entry remains at `docs/adj-web/release/web-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`. CAA-012 can be used to verify whether the current entry has collection or execution records; do not backfill zero when there is no evidence. The independent event stream in CAA-004 preserves the page state from the window; the daily report keeps only the link. If the old route must be restored, find the snapshot first, then revert it; without a snapshot, stop—do not guess the old destination.

This checklist still covers the exit action, the last visible result, and the exit record in adj-web. It does not resolve what "the entry point can be opened but the current result does not finish" means, nor does it confirm the release on behalf of the corresponding owner.

# Alternative Plan for Caller Integration Testing

This proposal has continued to be used to explain an approach that was not adopted: whether to split the caller integration-testing records out from beside the current entry point. It preserves the comparison made at the time, not a description of the later integration-testing process. The old wording, "keep a separate record," remains because people come here to trace why the idea did not move forward at the time.

The original idea was narrow: keep the request and current revision near the current entry point; when a cross-entry-point recheck was needed, keep a separate record for web-client-integration. Those in favor of the split worried about different exit points being mixed together; those against it worried that the records in the second location would have no consistent users. No conclusion was drawn from either side's concerns at the time, and no arrangements to begin were confirmed.

During a later follow-up check, a screenshot of the internal view was once treated as user-side evidence. That judgment no longer applies. The screenshot did not cover the user's return from the exit entry point, so it can only help locate the current entry point; it cannot establish what calls were made through the public entry point. The short-term comparison proposed on this basis in the old version should not be understood as a trial that had already been carried out.

Scattered notes on the cards made the issue more concrete. CAA-002 require fetching the first current revision as the first step after recovery; CAA-005 warn that the trends before and after a change to the current entry point cannot be directly subtracted from one another. Taken together, these two points support only a conservative comparison: first mark the entry-point change, then examine the records from each starting point separately. The two series of numbers cannot be stitched into a single trend. The earlier `dependency_checked` was later confirmed to have been mixed up with a misplaced expiry action, so it is no longer used as evidence that the dependency was confirmed.

CAA-007 require another check at the public entry point using the original web-client-integration. Local rechecks are used to locate possible requests and exit points; only results from the public entry point address whether the caller can actually complete the original path. If neither location has a result, leave it blank. Here, "blank" is not a finding of failure, nor is it a gap that can be filled with a screenshot.

The plan that was not adopted at the time could have been narrowed as follows, rather than moving all Web callers to a new set of records:

- Continue to use the current entry point as the starting point for every recheck;
- Attach a separate web-client-integration record only to requests that need to be reviewed from the exit entry point;
- Stop expanding the sample set if the input fields have not been confirmed by the upstream interface owner;
- When the current entry point changes, first save the records in separate segments, then decide whether a comparison is needed;
- Do not adjust the scope of callers on this basis until the public entry point recheck is complete.

These conditions addressed "whether a trial was possible" at the time; they were not a decision on "what should be adopted permanently." The last item is particularly relevant: CAA-010 require confirming the teams still using adj-web and the exit conditions; if no consumers can be found, still retain only the query scope. It did not provide a list of consumers, so finalizing the scope cannot be written up as a completed migration.

Another disagreement remained unresolved during review: should the separate record be tied to the request or to the exit entry point? The former makes it easier to look back from the current entry point, but scatters records for the same exit point; the latter brings exit issues together, but requires every caller to be able to explain why it would reach that exit. The available material does not cover either approach end to end, so there is no basis for presenting them as validated design choices.

The rollback conditions are also spelled out more clearly than in the old version. If the public entry point and local records do not match, the input fields remain unconfirmed, or the split-out records prevent people from getting back to the original entry point, remove the added records and return to the current entry point. This proposal does not invalidate the original entry point; the candidate records are only supplementary navigation aids. The lack of results at both locations described in CAA-015 should still be recorded as unknown; do not infer that a caller has already exited just to bring the comparison to a close.

This approach was ultimately not adopted, but that does not mean splitting the records was itself proven wrong. What it lacked at the time was a recheck at the public entry point, confirmed input fields, and a clearly defined scope of adoption; expanding record coverage further before filling these gaps would only make the internal view and the user-side path harder to compare. Related material can still be found at `docs/adj-web/proposals/unused-Web-client-integration-route.md`.

# Quality Signal Desk FAQ

All three questions left by users concern the same point: where to read failed samples produced by test and spec, who will continue maintaining regression layering and unstable-signal attribution, and whether the page at hand represents the current revision. The confirmed entry points are kept here; unsupported parts are not turned into conclusions.

## Where is the current entry point

Start with `docs/adj-infra/faq/infra-quality-signal-board-three-user-questions.md`. This is the infra · Quality Signal Board knowledge base's latest-known export. The page body and attachments are still maintained by adj-infra, so the export page is useful for locating issues and reading existing records, but should not be treated as a copy detached from project maintenance.

The current records place failed samples at the boundary between test and spec: first distinguish which regression layer a sample belongs to, then check whether the unstable signal has been attributed. These two things are not merged into a single status. The former indicates which regression category the sample is placed in; the latter may still be only a signal awaiting confirmation.

## Which revision is current

The available material labels this entry only as latest-known; it does not provide a specific revision name that can be restated on this page. So the answer for "current revision" is: use the project's body and attachments referenced by the export page, not an excerpt from the page.

The existing records in the export show `SQLite readiness` and `TodosVm`; content after `Web.AcceptanceTests` has not been recorded here. This cutoff only indicates where the material visible on this page ends; it cannot be used to determine whether subsequent tests passed, nor can results from administrators or internal environments be extrapolated to ordinary users. If the page content and attachments disagree, retain the discrepancy and return to the project-maintained body to verify it; do not choose one side to overwrite the other on the FAQ page.

## What to carry over when taking over

The Quality Signal Desk has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria. The person taking over needs to carry forward the test or spec to which the failed sample belongs, the regression layer it was placed in, and whether the unstable signal has been attributed yet; do not carry over only a "failed" label.

If the signal has not been attributed, record it as still awaiting attribution; do not write it up as a confirmed regression just to hand it over.

This page contains no confirmable individual name or fixed handoff window. If further follow-up is needed, use the entry point above to check the maintenance information in the body and attachments; arrangements outside the page are not entered here.

## Open questions

- Whether there is another attachment for records after `Web.AcceptanceTests` is unanswered on this page.
- Whether the regression layer for a particular unstable sample should be adjusted requires the sample's actual record first.
- If the content users read differs from the entry point, first preserve the location of the first difference, then send that discrepancy to the project maintainers for confirmation.

# Quality Signal Hub Incident Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

The "stuck" reports received by the Quality Signal Hub are usually only a symptom: failed samples for a test or spec are no longer being produced, existing samples do not match the regression stratification, or same-named objects are being compared without clarifying which version they are. Do not combine these phenomena into a single cause yet. The procedure here is to move downward from the current entry; each time, follow only one branch supported by existing evidence, and stop at the first point where new material is required.

The entry file is still at `docs/adj-infra/runbooks/infra-quality-signal-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`. When taking over, first confirm that the record on hand came from that entry, then check whether the record contains the original input, current result, and version identifier. Attachments are still maintained by the Quality Signal Hub; the person taking over is not required to fill in the history first, only to avoid replacing the state at the time with content generated later.

## Freeze the current state first

Write the phenomenon currently observed as a sentence that can be rechecked, such as "a test's failed sample did not appear again" or "the spec result does not match the most recently known state." Do not use "it is stuck" in place of the phenomenon, and do not initially write it as a conclusion about an interface, cache, or permissions.

Then check three things: the original input, the current result, and the version identifier. The original input is the content that triggered this round of collection or execution; the current result is the earliest result left by this round. If any one of them is missing, this only means that the evidence is incomplete; files from another round cannot be used to fill it in. When the version identifier is missing, old objects with the same name, infra-quality-signal, must be retained separately; do not assume they are the same based on their names.

```text
Does the current entry have an original record?
├─ No
│  ├─ Can the original input for this round be found: add the original input and first visible result to the record
│  └─ Cannot find the original input for this round: record it as a gap, stop; do not discuss the root cause
└─ Yes
   ├─ The original input and current result belong to the same round: check the version identifier
   └─ The round is unclear or inconsistent: save them separately, stop comparing
```

The "original record" here does not require a uniform format. Command output, test logs, trace snippets, or diff snippets can all be part of the evidence, as long as they indicate which round they came from. If all that remains is a curated green result, do not treat it as recovery from the failure; it can only show that some later execution did not present the same phenomenon again.

If it has not yet been confirmed whether collection or execution actually occurred, the current revision remains unknown. Do not fill in a revision just because the entry file exists, a same-named object exists, or someone says "it should have run." An unknown version is a state that must be retained, not a placeholder that can be filled in casually while waiting.

## Decide whether the sample can remain in the project

After the evidence is fixed, first look at where the first clear difference falls. For the comparison, choose only one recent normal sample, and first compare the input, version identifier, and first result; do not infer the intermediate process from averages, directory names, or the last displayed state. Each comparison should answer only one question: does the difference remain within the Quality Signal Hub's handling scope for test, spec, regression stratification, or unstable-signal attribution?

```text
Can the first difference be located?
├─ Cannot locate
│  ├─ Record whether the missing item is the input, result, version, or round
│  └─ Stop; do not hand it off to a specific maintainer
└─ Can locate
   ├─ Within the test/spec sample, stratification, or unstable-signal attribution: keep it in infra-quality-signal
   ├─ In an exit action: record the first difference before and after the action, then follow the exit branch
   └─ In resource access or permission denial: follow the permissions branch
```

"Keep it in infra-quality-signal" does not mean rerun it immediately. First retain the first failing sample, related input, version identifier, and environmental differences. Older records treated premature retries as recovery actions, which hid the first failure; now a retry may be performed only after the original evidence has been retained. Record the result after the retry separately; do not overwrite the original input or result.

Record environmental differences only when they are the first visible difference. The current result after a cold cache can be attached separately to the record, but it does not replace the original result associated with the expiration action. When a change appears only after a cold cache, place both results side by side first; do not retroactively modify the old conclusion. If there is no evidence that the two came from the same round, do not compare them directly.

## Exit-action branch

An exit action is the point at which troubleshooting can no longer be supported by internal Quality Signal Hub material and must leave the current branch. It is not synonymous with "we have not thought of it yet." Stop at that node when any of the following occurs:

- The first difference has been confirmed to cross the current interface, and further judgment must depend on material from the other side of the interface;
- The user-visible contract needs to be changed, but the records on hand contain only failed samples;
- The original input, current result, or version identifier is missing, so any further comparison would mix in another round;
- Old objects with the same name cannot be distinguished by version, and no usable version record exists.

When stopping, leave four minimum items: the current entry, the last confirmed branch, what material is missing, and the location of the originals already retained. Do not write "it may be some interface" as a definite attribution. If the difference has in fact crossed an explicit interface, give these four items to the maintainer of that interface; if the names are merely similar and there is no interface evidence, remain in the current record and do not route it out as a shared issue.

A new investigation record may be created after the exit action, but do not append a string of guesses to the end of the original branch. The new record should start only from the last confirmed point. This allows the next person taking over to see which content came from the evidence and which material has not yet been obtained.

## Permissions branch

A permissions issue requires seeing where access was denied. The fact that collection did not occur, a result did not appear, or an object is not visible is not by itself enough to hand it off as a permissions issue. First retain the input used when access was denied and the first result; if the record contains only a retelling that there was "no permission," with no corresponding location, return to the "original record missing" branch.

```text
Is there a clear access-denial location?
├─ No: fill in the evidence; cannot attribute it to permissions
└─ Yes
   ├─ The denial occurred in the Quality Signal Hub's own resource: handle it within the project
   └─ The denial occurred in a resource requiring external authorization: hand it to the maintainer responsible for that permission
```

When handing off the permissions branch, there is no need to decide on the maintainer's behalf how authorization should be changed. The handoff should contain only the denied location, the original input for this round, the first result, the known version identifier, and an indication of whether collection or execution has been confirmed to have occurred. If an authorization change would alter the behavior of the current interface, stop here; do not write a change plan on this page.

## Reproduction by a second person

When a second colleague reproduces the issue, they should use only the material already in the current ticket and follow the tree. The person reproducing it should not supply an input that "looks similar" just to make the steps work, nor splice in the current result from another round. When there is a gap, write it next to the original step: missing original input, missing current result, missing version identifier, unclear round, or no access-denial location.

The value of reproduction is to confirm that the branch can reach the same stopping point using the same set of material, not to prove the ultimate cause. If both people stop at the same gap, the next step is to obtain that missing material; if they stop at different branches, first compare whether the original inputs and current results each used belong to the same round. Until this is confirmed, do not use "the second person could not reproduce it" as a reason to escalate.

For samples that can already be handled within the project, the second person only needs to verify that the first difference and retained artifacts are consistent. At permissions or interface boundaries, the second person should verify that the handoff conditions have been met, rather than continuing the investigation for the external maintainer.

## Legacy records and later additions

If an old page described the green result after a rerun as recovery, retain the original sentence beside it and append the current explanation: the green result came from a later execution and cannot overwrite the initial failure. If an old page directly treated two same-named objects as the same object, do not delete the old record; add an explanation that the version identifier is missing and separate the old objects.

CAB-009 recorded the missing version identifier for the same-named infra-quality-signal and the separate handling of old objects; CAB-010 retained the practice of keeping the revision unknown when collection or execution has not been confirmed. Materials added later to the two tickets also made clear that the original input and current result cannot be compared across rounds, and that the result after a cold cache should be saved separately. CAB-011 are used for a second person to reproduce using only the material in the ticket and write the gap next to the step; CAB-012 are used to preserve the temporal context of an old judgment and then append the new result side by side.

These additions change the judgments available when following the tree; they do not rewrite the early evidence as a verified conclusion. Current entry: which record location in the Quality Signal Hub
```text
Last confirmed: where the first difference is, or which item of material is missing
Retained content: original input / current result / version identifier / first failing sample
Handoff reason: crossed an explicit interface, or an access-denial location in an external resource has appeared
```

If the conditions in the last line have not been met, do not assign a maintainer just to clear the queue. Samples internal to the Quality Signal Hub should remain in the project for handling; as long as the first difference has not gone beyond the current scope, continue adding sample, stratification, or attribution material. The place where it is truly necessary to leave should be evident from the evidence already retained.

# Dependency Boundary Entry-Point Migration Index

This index is organized by migration batch; the tradeoff between `ValueObject` and `WebApi` is no longer treated as the sole organizing thread. The previous version only noted that the two sides had different failure exits; the replacement location, callers still working through the old entry point, and exit responsibility now need to be recorded separately.

The scope is application-supply-boundary: dependency sources built around license and security, together with adoption scope and exit responsibility. Each item has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit conditions. Explanations that cannot be traced back are marked as expired first; do not fill them in from adjacent items.

```text
Before migration
Old entry point ───────────> Callers still using it
   │                         │
   │ Keep a recoverable record │ Confirm batch by batch
   ▼                         ▼
Replacement location ─────────> Callers confirmed migrated

Rollback: Stop this batch and restore affected callers to the old entry point
```

## How to Record an Item

An index item records a change in the lookup path; it is not itself a dependency. At minimum, list:

- The old entry point and replacement location;
- Callers confirmed to still be using the old entry point;
- The adoption scope for trial use, compatibility retention, or completed migration;
- The maintainer, an independent schedule, and exit conditions;
- Any old notes left when the history cannot be traced back.

"Current entry point" means the location where a caller currently looks up and registers it; it is not determined by the file creation time. The "old entry point" is the location that existed before migration. Both can coexist. Only when the replacement location, caller confirmation, and historical lookup are all available can migration completion be assessed.

## Low-Traffic Phase

For CAC-003, the constraint is to replace only one adjacent application-supply-boundary, leaving all other current entry points and entries untouched. A batch replaces only the source it is handling; all other entry points and callers remain unchanged. That is the only way to tell which item a change belongs to.

First mark a caller as using the replacement location on a trial basis; the old entry point remains readable, searchable, or recoverable. Trial use does not mean migrated. Only after confirming that it can find the same dependency source, adoption scope, and exit notes may its status change. Simply seeing the replacement location appear does not change the caller's status.

## Access Anomaly

In the records for CAC-006, access to adj-application by a regular identity was interrupted before an execution record was created; the adjacent item's current result remains normal. They cannot be combined as "migration successful." Keep the denial location and request/run id on the original card; the index records only that caller verification is incomplete and whether the old entry point is still usable.

Move explanatory text with no execution record into the expired notes. Keep the original entry point and original object; do not use directory structure or adjacent results to fill in a reason. Once access is restored, verify the old entry point and replacement location separately.

## Rollback

Rollback applies to a single batch. If the replacement location cannot preserve the original lookup relationship, stop further migration and mark affected callers back as either still using the old entry point or pending recheck; retain the new location and failure symptoms. The caller Fang Ke whose old path has been confirmed usable is marked back to the old entry point; callers whose old path has not been confirmed either can only remain pending recheck.

The handoff entry is still `docs/adj-application/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. CAC-003 and CAC-006 are for navigation, not a replacement for the caller ledger here.

# Dependency Boundary Entry Migration Index

This index records how a dependency source changes its lookup location and which callers still depend on the old entry during the migration. It is not a copy of the dependency catalog. Within application-supply-boundary, the sources associated with license and security, their scopes of use, and their exit responsibilities must each be recorded in separate index entries; an alternative location appearing in the catalog only means that the location has been prepared, not that the callers have been migrated.

The entry where this record can currently be found is `docs/adj-application/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. The old description has not been cleared. Sections where the source, caller, or execution record cannot be found may remain, but they must be separated from the valid fields and marked as expired. When someone takes over later, check the location relationships first, then the caller status; do not infer that the entire item is complete from a single line containing a new path.

## First distinguish the four location relationships

**Old entry** is the location callers used before the migration to look up the dependency source, scope of use, or exit description. It may continue to provide lookups during the migration, or become the current entry again after a rollback.

**Alternative location** is the location prepared to take over this registration content. It may initially serve only one trial caller; its creation does not automatically take over other sources or other callers.

**Current entry** is the registration location that callers should look up at this moment. It is not the same as the "most recently created location." After a batch is rolled back, the old entry may become the current entry again; the alternative location may also be valid only for specifically named callers.

**Compatible caller** is a user that still needs to look up the source through the old entry during the migration. This does not mean that the caller has accepted the alternative location. It can be marked as migrated only after confirming that the same source, scope of use, and exit description can be found at the alternative location.

Exit responsibility is recorded separately as well. It answers when the old entry can stop being maintained, rather than generically stating who is responsible for the project. Each source has its own maintainer, independent schedule, and exit criteria. When the caller status is unknown, the exit criteria cannot be recorded as satisfied.

## Order for writing an index entry

When filling in an entry, first preserve the existing wording from the old entry, then write the new lookup location. Here, "preserve" means retaining the content as it was at that time, not rewriting the old description in current wording. If the original wording can no longer be verified, note that it is expired beside it; do not directly reuse its conclusion in the current fields.

Then list the callers under four categories: still using the old entry, trying the alternative location, confirmed migrated, and pending recheck. The last category must be listed separately. If you have only seen the alternative location and have not seen that the caller actually switched to it, write pending recheck rather than putting it in the migrated column. A caller also cannot be represented by writing only a project name instead of the specific entry relationship; enter caller names only when known, and leave unknowns blank.

Next write the scope of use. Trial means that the new location has been assigned to the caller, but the old entry remains a recoverable path. Compatibility retained means that the caller has not completed the switch. Migrated means that the lookup, scope of use, and exit description have all been confirmed at the alternative location. Do not merge these three statuses just because they have the same batch name.

Finally, write the maintenance and exit information. The exit criteria should reflect the actual status of the item, such as the callers in this batch having migrated or the source no longer being used. Do not write only "The new entry has been created." If the maintainer or time window changes, append the new responsibility after the original entry while retaining the old record.

The following small diagram can be used to view the relationships in a migration batch:

```text
Old entry ──────────────> Compatible callers
   │                         │
   │ Original description retained; can be rolled back   │ Verify by batch
   ▼                         ▼
Alternative location ─────────────> Trial / migrated callers
             │
             └── Return to old entry on failure
```

## Choices left by the first version

The earliest record framed the issue as a choice between `ValueObject` and `WebApi`. What could be confirmed at the time was that the two sides had different failure paths, so the initial preference was to split out `WebApi` separately. This judgment remains as historical background, but it did not answer whether `acceptance-host` still has active callers, nor whether a rollback should restore only the references or the original description as well.

This question was not later rewritten as a completed conclusion. It directly affects whether the old entry can be retired: as long as the usage of `acceptance-host` has not been rechecked, the item cannot be changed from recoverable to deletable. The two old names are not automatically merged either; they may appear in separate index entries unless the corresponding caller relationships have been confirmed.

Therefore, the current migration completion condition is no longer "select `ValueObject` or `WebApi`." The name choice only explains how the records are split. What must actually be checked is whether callers can find the correct source, scope of use, and exit description. If only the catalog adjustment is completed, the index should remain in migration.

## Where to start a batch

Before starting, copy the source description, scope of use, callers, and exit description already present in the old entry, then identify the callers that truly need to be migrated in this batch. If the copied result contains expired content, retain the original wording and mark it separately. Do not let the blank space at the new location make it appear that the old content no longer exists.

Clearly state which source item the alternative location is taking over. It does not automatically take over adjacent items or automatically change the scope of the surrounding project. When one source involves both license and security, whether to process it in the same batch still depends on its actual scope of use; similar wording is not a reason to merge them.

Prioritize a batch item with clear callers and findable exit responsibility, rather than the item whose catalog is easiest to change. List the callers at the old entry before migration; after trial use begins, retain both the old-entry relationship and the alternative-location relationship. The trial-stage record should answer "Where do we retrieve the original description if something goes wrong?" rather than leaving only the new path.

During the trial, check three local facts: whether the caller can find the source at the alternative location, whether the scope of use still matches the old entry, and whether the exit description can be found. If only the first fact holds and the other two are missing, it is still a trial. If the old-entry description was already expired, the new location cannot directly turn it into a valid conclusion; it can only be recorded as pending confirmation.

At the end of a batch, retain the differences before and after migration: which compatible callers remain at the old entry, which confirmed callers were added at the alternative location, and which callers are blocked because they could not be rechecked. Do not use one batch result to overwrite these statuses.

## The batch whose access was denied

The access record for CAC-006 requires trying adj-application using a non-administrator identity, and leaving the denial location and the request/run id on the original card. Subsequent observation showed that the current result for the adjacent item was normal, but this item stopped before the execution record. A neighboring item being normal only shows that the neighboring item is normal; it does not prove that this item's alternative location is usable.

When access with a regular-user identity fails, the index should retain the in-progress migration status. Record the location where the denial occurred in CAC-006, leaving the request/run id; do not create another final success or failure status here. If the caller can still read the old entry, continue to mark it as a compatible caller; if the old entry has not been confirmed either, mark it as pending recheck. These two situations cannot both be called rolled back.

CAC-006 later had a completion action, but the action record does not replace the execution record for this access. The index should follow the actual denial location left behind and the caller status. If the new explanation has no execution record, move it from the valid descriptions to the expired section; do not use the neighboring item's result to fill the gap.

CAC-003 also left a constraint for adjacent replay: change only one adjacent application-supply-boundary, and leave the remaining Current Entry and Entry unchanged. This constraint can be used to define the batch scope. During replay, change only the target source; do not also change other entries or other callers, or the migration result cannot be attributed to a specific index entry.

## Old descriptions without execution records

An old description in the index may have stated that a caller had completed the switch, or may have explained why an access attempt was interrupted. If the corresponding execution record cannot now be found, the original wording may remain beside the old entry, but it cannot continue to appear in the valid fields. Specifically, retain the original wording, original object, and original location, and add an expired marker stating that the execution record has not yet been found.

This is not deleting history, nor is it finding a new reason for the old description. If the record is found later, it can be checked again; until then, the scope of use should rely only on confirmed callers and locations. In particular, do not restore the old explanation as a current fact merely because a file with the same name appears in the catalog.

The same handling applies to a rollback determination. If the old entry was once written as recoverable, but it has not now even been confirmed that the old path is readable, it can only be marked as pending recheck. Deactivating the alternative location does not mean that the caller has successfully returned to the old entry.

## Rolling back a batch

A rollback applies only to the callers in the current batch. Migration may be stopped when the alternative location cannot maintain the original lookup relationship, access validation is stuck before the execution record, or exit responsibility has not yet been clarified. Stopping does not require deleting the alternative location; retain it and the local records that caused the stop.

First relabel the affected callers as still using the old entry or pending recheck. Callers for which it has been confirmed that the old path can continue working belong in the former category; callers for which the old path is likewise unverified belong in the latter. Then restore to the old entry the source description, scope of use, and exit description needed for this batch. If the old description has expired, restore it only as a historical lookup location, not as the unverified conclusion it contains.

The alternative location should retain the record of this batch stopping and state the local reason, such as access not reaching the execution record or the caller not completing the recheck. After the rollback, check three things: whether the caller is still listed in the migrated section of the alternative location, whether the old entry retains the compatibility description, and whether the exit criteria were incorrectly left marked as satisfied. The first is migration status, the second is the recovery path, and the third is responsibility status; they cannot be covered by one "rolled back" status.

## Changes to the responsibility window

CAC-016 was later moved to be handled in an offline window and removed from the board. This action means that the board no longer carries the processing for this item; it does not mean that the old entry has been retired, nor that the caller has been confirmed complete automatically. The index should append the location where the current responsibility and exit time are confirmed, while retaining the original migration status.

When the responsibility window changes, the new maintainer takes over the specific source and batch, not all unknown items in the index. Existing caller confirmations can be carried forward; callers without confirmation remain pending recheck. If the exit time has not been confirmed, do not write a date placeholder in the exit criteria, and do not treat offline processing as approval to delete the old entry.

## When the old entry can be stopped

Only after the corresponding item satisfies the following local facts should you consider stopping maintenance of the old entry: the alternative location has taken over the source registration; the relevant callers have confirmed migration or are no longer using it; the scope of use and exit description can be found; the maintainer and independent schedule are clear; and there are no pending-recheck gaps in the access or execution records.

When compatible callers still exist, the old entry continues to exist. It is not unusual for different sources to be at different stages: one item may finish while another still needs to retain the old path. Maintaining the old entry also does not mean canceling the new migration; it only means that the item has not yet met the exit criteria.

Do not treat card status, catalog changes, or responsibility-window changes alone as exit signals. Each provides only local information. CAC-003, CAC-006, and CAC-016 are used respectively to navigate adjacent replay, regular-user access, and the responsibility window; the final accounts for the old entry, alternative location, and callers are still maintained in this index.

During handoff, use `docs/adj-application/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md` to find the specific index entry. First confirm which license or security source it registers, then check whether the caller is in trial, compatibility retained, migrated, or pending recheck. Sources with similar names are not automatically merged, and expired descriptions are not automatically restored.

# Runtime Observability Maintainer Map

This map supports handoffs during operation; it is not meant to assign a catch-all owner for `domain-operations-observability`. Material coming into Domain · Operations Observability Board often combines runtime signals, failure context, and recovery observation windows. Some of it needs to be picked up by the person on duty first, while some must wait for a long-term assessment from the relevant implementation area. Putting all three kinds of action in one cell makes it hard to tell later who took over temporarily, who should continue handling the work at exit, and who has not yet been assigned by name.

We currently use the following boundary: `domain-operations-observability`, exit actions, and temporary takeover actions are routed separately; Domain · Operations Observability Board does not draw technical conclusions on behalf of the long-term owner.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M[Runtime signals produced by monitor] --> W[Domain · Operations Observability Board on-duty intake]
    F[Failure context] --> W
    R[Recovery observation window] --> W
    W --> Q{Action indicated by the material}
    Q -->|Current entry point| N[Current action handler]
    Q -->|Exit action| X[Exit action handler]
    Q -->|Temporary takeover| H[Temporary handler]
    N --> L[Relevant long-term owner]
    X --> L
    H --> P{Long-term owner confirmed?}
    P -->|Yes| L
    P -->|No| B[Retain blank slot and expiration details]
```

| Item to route | Initial handoff destination | When to hand off to the long-term owner | What the map should retain |
|---|---|---|---|
| `domain-operations-observability` current entry point | Domain · Operations Observability Board on-duty person | When implementation behavior, risk, or scope needs to be explained | Current entry point and minimum observed symptoms |
| Exit action | Relevant exit action handler | When the public entry point is still failing, or the exit decision goes beyond the scope of on-duty actions | Local result, public entry point result, exit status |
| Temporary takeover action | Temporary handler | When the temporary assignment expires or the long-term owner has been confirmed | Handler, expiration details, blank slot for long-term responsibility |
| Issue in another implementation area | Maintenance entry point for the relevant implementation area | When the issue has been confirmed to be outside the original implementation area | Original entry point, reason for the handoff, and failure-context snippets |
| Index timing discrepancy | Current action handler | When the ordering of the index and the object cannot be explained | Both time points, without forcing an attribution of responsibility |

The "person on duty" in the table is a receiving point, not a substitute for technical responsibility. After receiving the material, the person on duty first determines whether it falls under the current entry point, exit actions, or temporary takeover actions. As soon as the issue goes beyond that interface, they pass the entry point, time, and minimum observed symptoms to the relevant maintenance destination. The person asking does not need to reconstruct the entire failure history. In turn, the handler should not just forward a message saying "recovered", because the next person needs to distinguish whether the recovery was in the local result or at the public entry point.

CAD-004 is where this boundary came up in practice. The early handoff had been confirmed, but the issue was later found to be in another implementation area, and the assignee was updated along with the card. That adjustment shows that the original handoff destination was no longer appropriate; it does not mean the original entry point was responsible for long-term technical judgments in that area. The follow-up results on the card were: the local result was back to normal; the public entry point corresponding to the exit entry point was still failing. The maintainer map therefore lists exit actions separately. Recovery on the local side alone does not allow the exit action to be crossed off the table. The symptoms of the public entry point failure should continue to be passed to the exit action handler along with the entry point name.

CAD-009 recorded another, narrower comparison method: choose a working adjacent current revision and compare only the first path difference. The toolchain had already been fixed in place, and the contact changed afterward. Here, "the toolchain is fixed" does not mean responsibility has stabilized; it only keeps toolchain changes out of the comparison between adjacent revisions. If the first path difference cannot be explained, stop there. Do not keep extending the maintenance scope along similarly named paths.

CAD-013 deals with the expiration of a temporary assignment. The map records only the current action handler and expiration details, leaving long-term responsibility blank. Expiration is not a reason to turn the temporary handler into the owner; if the receiving party has not yet been confirmed, leave both the blank slot and the unfinished action in place. This way, after the recovery observation window ends, it is still clear who is responsible for the wrap-up actions and who has not yet taken responsibility for long-term judgments.

Index issues are kept off to the side. CAD-004 had flagged that the indexing time and `domain-operations-observability` might be in reverse order; any unexplained timing difference must remain in the record. It should not be used to infer who is responsible for an action. DOC-39 is a navigation point for the migration index for the old entry point. You can start there when looking up the index, but the migration guidance in DOC-39 does not replace the current handoff relationships in this map.

The slots currently left blank are not omissions: when the long-term owner has not been confirmed, a blank is more accurate than filling in the person who replied most recently. Material that needs a technical conclusion still goes to the relevant long-term owner; material requiring follow-through on the current action is handled by the on-duty or temporary handler. Both types of material can appear at the same time, and they should not be folded into one answer just because both are on the Runtime Observability Console.
