# SDK image refresh decision record

This item first entered the discussion under the name SDK image refresh. The name brings the image itself to mind first, but the recurring disagreement during the window was actually whether to also adjust the domain-valueobjects entry point during the refresh. Scheduling both actions in the same round does not mean they can be approved on the same grounds.

The initial draft left only "Keep the old entry point for now". At the time, that sentence was enough to prevent an overly broad consolidation, but it did not explain why the entry point had become an issue for the window, or record the reasons for setting aside the other approach. The later review did not turn this into an entry point migration decision; it added the scope on which that trade-off depended, and what it meant to keep the old entry point as a rollback point.

## The two approaches on the table at the time

The first approach was to proceed with the refresh while keeping the existing domain-valueobjects entry point available. Which locations the refresh needed to involve would be determined by the actual checks during the window; the old entry point would not automatically disappear as a result of the image work.

The second approach was to use the window to adjust the entry point. This appeared to allow the refresh and directory cleanup to be completed together, making the handoff seem like just one remaining task. But once the entry point moved, the discussion would no longer be limited to image selection: the locations used to trace back through the repository tree, the conventions still visible externally, and where clients start could all need to be explained together.

The difference between the two approaches was not which name looked tidier. Keeping the entry point left the unconfirmed parts where they were; adjusting it required this round to clearly document the impact across several aspects. The former left room to keep moving forward, while the latter could only be considered for a decision if there was enough supporting material.

Before the meeting, someone had reviewed the records by following `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/components/Home.js` and the call names refresh, platform, and client. This location helped bring the discussion back to the client side, but it was not treated as the entry point's permanent home, nor was this location alone used to infer that all client paths were already the same.

## Decision for this round

What was approved for this round was: keep the existing domain-valueobjects entry point while continuing preparation and coordination for the SDK image refresh. There can be an adjustment window, and a review can be scheduled; it does not come with permission to "replace the entry point while we are at it".

This does not designate the old entry point as a long-term structure. The immediate reason for keeping it is that rollback needs a clear destination. If coordination after the refresh reveals that the public contract still depends on the old name, or that a client startup path still goes through the old location, handling the issue can return to an already clearly defined object rather than reconstructing the previous connections on the fly.

The decision also limits the scope of approval. The repository tree, public contract, and client startup paths must be viewed as one integration surface, not three unrelated checklists. Merely confirming that files still exist in a directory cannot replace an assessment of the public conventions; merely seeing a client start does not establish that the old trace-back path is no longer in use. Approval extends only as far as the available material covers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[SDK image refresh] --> B[Keep the domain-valueobjects entry point]
    A --> C[Adjustment window]
    B --> D[Old entry point available for rollback]
    C --> E[Actual impact record]
    E --> F[Repository tree]
    E --> G[Public contract]
    E --> H[Client startup paths]
```

The diagram does not indicate that changing the entry point during the adjustment window has been approved. It only preserves the relationships at the time: the refresh and the window both touch the same area of discussion, while the old entry point is the part that can be returned to during the window.

## Arguments that were not adopted

"The window is short, so doing the entry point cleanup at the same time is easier" was not accepted. It treated convenience in coordination as evidence that the impact was already understood. The window can determine when people focus on the issues together, but it cannot replace an assessment of the issues themselves. If replacing the entry point changes both the public contract and client startup paths, squeezing both actions into one time period does not reduce what needs to be confirmed.

"If the client does not report an error immediately, the entry point can be removed" was not used as a basis either. Client startup paths are only one side of the integration surface. A client being able to start may only show that its own connection works; it does not establish a conclusion about the old trace-back locations in the repository tree, or about consumers of the public contract. This argument was later often remembered as "look at the client first", but its original intent was only to treat the client as an entry point that could expose connection issues relatively early.

There was also a tendency to avoid window adjustments altogether and reduce the refresh to an image-only operation. This was not written into the final direction either. The adjustment window was a real coordination condition and could not be treated as nonexistent; its role in this decision was simply narrowed to scheduling review and handoff, rather than endorsing entry point migration.

The sentence "Discuss window adjustments separately" from the initial draft was therefore retained. At the time, it prevented unverified cleanup from being bundled into the refresh, but quoting it on its own could lead people to think that the window itself was unimportant, or that the entry point could never be changed. Both readings go beyond the original decision.

## Limits added during review

After review, the focus of the decision changed from "preserve compatibility" to a more specific statement: the old entry point is kept so that the rollback boundary for this round can be explained, not to declare that compatibility work is complete. The entry point continuing to exist does not mean every client still needs it; the entry point not having moved does not mean the public conventions have all been checked individually.

The review material required the handoff to record actual impact, a coordinator, and reproducible checks. Here, actual impact refers only to repository locations, public conventions, or startup connection points that were actually checked or changed during this refresh. Areas that might be affected but have not yet been reviewed cannot become "affected" simply by being included in a handoff record.

The coordinator is responsible for bringing cross-aspect issues arising in the same round back into the discussion; this does not mean that person takes over subsequent maintenance of all objects. Reproducible checks likewise only allow the recipient to determine whether the connection in this round still holds without relying on verbal recollections; they are not proof claiming coverage of all clients. The initial draft did not name a specific coordinator, so this review did not retroactively insert a later contact person into that point in time either.

One statement used at the time was: every handoff should specify an owner and reproducible checks. The term handoff is retained here because, in the meeting, it specifically referred to the handoff activity within the window. It requires a clear destination for what is handed off, not a single record that replaces the separate maintenance relationships for all objects.

## Items that need to be recorded in the handoff

The old entry point field should state whether it is still retained and what location can be returned to if coordination issues arise. The repository tree field should record only the scope actually inspected or touched in this round. The public contract field should explain whether the existing visible conventions still need to be maintained. The client startup paths field should list the connection points checked in this round, without inferring that other clients have no independent entry points.

The coordination record should keep cross-aspect issues within the same round: for example, whether the entry point name is still referenced by public conventions, or whether client startup bypasses the original path. It does not need to turn every potential issue into a task in advance, nor can it falsely claim that an issue has disappeared just because a field is still blank.

Reproducible checks should closely match the objects described in this handoff. Checking an old location in the repository tree, checking public conventions, or checking a client startup connection yields results only for the corresponding side. If all three sides are within this round's scope, results should be recorded separately for each; if only one side has been confirmed, the record should cover only that side as well.

## The earlier judgment still retained

> Keep the old entry point for now, and discuss window adjustments separately.

This sentence still helps explain why the two actions were not combined at the time. It should not be treated as an operating rule for all subsequent SDK image refresh work. If later refreshes involve different public contracts, different client startup paths, or already have complete impact records, the approaches need to be compared again rather than using this round's decision to retain the entry point as a direct substitute for judgment.

Similarly, "start by looking at the client" remains a useful starting point for investigation, but it is no longer the full sequence described by this decision. It can provide quick feedback, but it can also obscure the old entry point in the repository tree and public contract. It is therefore retained here as a tendency that appeared during review, not as a new process requirement.

## Matters left outside the decision

This record does not confirm whether the entry point adjustment was ultimately implemented, nor does it list the clients after the refresh. Those details were outside the approved scope at the time. The gaps are preserved so that "no changes were made in this round" is not misread as "it has been verified that no changes are needed".

DOC-44 separately records the handoff for the Aspire environment window. Both pages mention a window, but the handoff status there cannot be used to infer the entry point decision here; what is preserved here is the trade-off made in that round of the SDK image refresh.

# aspire-host Preview Entry Code-Reading Notes

This note originally followed one entry point downward from the repository's public entry at aspire-host, with a targeted review added later. When reading the code, don't first group configuration files with similar names in the workspace side by side; start by selecting one direct call edge that has already been observed, then see where it actually leads. This preserves the basis for the judgment made at the time and avoids mistaking search results for call relationships.

The file currently confirmed is `src/Web/ClientApp/proxy.conf.js`. The `host` in that file is a connection clue left along this narrow path. It led the search to the web client side and showed that there is a location near the entry point that needs further tracing; by itself, it does not provide enough information to determine permanent ownership of the frontend preview slot. The file location here is also not the result of merging all same-named configurations; it is only the local point where this entry trace actually stopped.

The path can first be drawn like this:

```text
aspire-host
    |
    v
one direct caller
    |
    v
src/Web/ClientApp/proxy.conf.js
    |
    v
host
    |
    v
the first actual consumer of the frontend preview slot
```

"one direct caller" in the diagram is not a caller inventory. It represents the one edge selected when starting from aspire-host. Only after following that edge into `proxy.conf.js` is there a basis for placing `host` on the route; the fact that another file contains the same name is not enough to connect it as the next hop. Same-named files without a call edge are still useful, but only as pointers for the search; they cannot stand in for the actual consumer or implementation location.

This is also where the word "entry" in the draft can easily be read too broadly. "Entry" refers to the starting point of this search and the first confirmed relationship; it does not mean that aspire-host has already explained the entire registration process for the frontend preview slot. `proxy.conf.js` only carries the local clue in this note and should not be read as a frontend route or slot inventory. Anyone continuing the search from here should follow the call edges that already exist rather than linking configuration files horizontally based on their wording.

During the review, acceptance replay served a locating function. Replaying the flow first so that the already observed entry appears again, then checking the client-side location through which the request passed, makes it possible to place the end of the route near the first actual consumer of the frontend preview slot. The replay helps confirm the search direction—"where it enters and where it is consumed"—but this note does not expand the replay into an acceptance result, nor does it infer whether the slot was available at the time from response content that was not recorded.

The actual follow-up check can be performed in the following steps, with each step limited to this route:

1. Start from the public entry of aspire-host and first identify the one direct caller to track. Fix this edge first, then move to the next file.
2. Open `src/Web/ClientApp/proxy.conf.js` and inspect `host` in the local context. Confirm how it carries forward the current route; do not generalize the file into an index of all frontend configuration.
3. Use acceptance replay to reproduce the entry already found, then observe whether the route reaches the location of the first actual consumer of the frontend preview slot. The replay is used only to locate this endpoint.
4. Keep wayfinding markers for same-named files without call edges; do not add an unseen edge just to make the route longer.
5. Stop at the last confirmed object when reaching a point that requires another owner's explanation. Leave the ownership question at this boundary rather than filling it in by guesswork.

After the second-pass review, the route still ends only at the first actual consumer. The material is sufficient to show how to get from aspire-host to `proxy.conf.js`, and sufficient to explain why `host` is worth investigating further; it is not sufficient to show complete ownership downstream of the slot, all callers, or runtime status. This gap is not resolved by listing more files. If a new call edge appears later, it should be attached beside the corresponding local relationship; if there is only a verbal explanation from another owner, that explanation still needs to be mapped to the actual entry first.

Two judgments that are easy to conflate are kept separate here: `host` is a valid search clue, not the owner of the preview slot; a same-named file is a wayfinding marker, not a caller. Acceptance replay can help confirm that the selected entry appears again; it does not automatically create a missing code relationship. Reviewing these three objects step by step can lead to the actual entry supported by the current material; continuing past the slot means stopping at the point where ownership clarification is still needed.

# SDK image refresh deviation postmortem

During the SDK image refresh window, the result observed on site did not match the original plan. The record does not label this as an incident with a confirmed root cause: the initial discovery, temporary recovery, and the parts that remained unknown afterward are kept separate. The actual impact is recorded first at the visible-scope level: during the shift, it was not possible to determine from the window schedule alone whether the SDK image had already switched, nor to treat the result shown by the old entry point as indicating that the refresh was complete. Whether any higher-level callers were affected was not confirmed at the time.

## On-site record

At the time, the investigation followed `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/service-worker.js` and used `image` for a follow-up check. This location exposed clues about local image handling, but it was not designated as the long-term ownership location, nor was a complete call chain inferred from it. A separate OpenAPI snapshot was also retained as the original artifact of the state visible during the window. The snapshot can show what the interface looked like when it was saved; it cannot by itself establish the actual refresh state of the SDK image.

## Timeline

- Before the window began, a plan for the SDK image refresh was already in place, with the expectation that the visible result during the window would match the plan.
- At first discovery, the result presented by the page or entry point did not match this plan. The discovery record did not include runtime logs sufficient to pin down the cause, so "a deviation occurred during the refresh window" was retained as the working hypothesis.
- The investigation continued along leads from `service-worker.js` and `image`, but it did not combine the old entry point, cache state, and actual image contents into a confirmed attribution.
- A temporary recovery was then completed, and the observed result returned to a state that could continue to be monitored; the recovery action itself did not prove which layer caused the initial deviation.
- What remained unconfirmed after recovery was whether the deviation occurred in the refresh of the SDK image, in the old entry point's display, or in the timing between the two. This gap remains in the postmortem; the recovery result was not used to infer the root cause retroactively.

## Old wording still on the page

Early records attributed the phenomenon only to "a refresh deviation during the window" and tended to wait for the result to align on its own. This assessment could help on-call staff handle it initially at the time, but it cannot be used as current operating guidance; it did not distinguish among image content, the old entry point, and the visible interface snapshot. The old wording is retained so later readers can see the boundary of what was understood at the time, not to polish it into a conclusion.

This update adds three operational control points: actual impact must be recorded in a separate field; the window coordinator needs a clearly identified place, currently recorded only as "window coordinator," and the name has not been confirmed on this page; temporary recovery must not remove the old entry point, which must remain available for rollback until the refresh state and entry-point state have been confirmed separately. It remains unresolved in this material which party will complete the impact scope and how long the old entry point should be retained after recovery.

# SDK image refresh FAQ

This page was written after the same questions kept coming up about SDK image refresh. The earliest records conflated one successful entry-point check with completion of the entire path; during later follow-up checks, `src/Web/ClientApp-React/src/service-worker.js` was also treated as a fixed location. That old assessment is retained here because it explains why the same question kept coming up, but it is no longer a basis for closing the work.

### What can the existing application-events entry point prove?

It can prove that the portion of local behavior observed by the native probe succeeded. On its own, it cannot prove that SDK image refresh has taken effect for neighboring callers, nor can the entry-point name establish responsibility for the client or host path. The v1 position that "entry-point success means completion" is outdated; v2 narrowed it to a single observation.

Finding an old file or seeing words such as image, work, client, or path only shows that someone looked in that location at the time. This page does not establish permanent ownership based on a file location, and that location must not substitute for a record of the candidate path's withdrawal. If the only evidence available is successful output from application-events, the issue is not complete enough to close.

### Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?

The old answer assigned responsibility for withdrawal to the SDK maintainers. The candidate path's owner did not confirm that answer. It is retained as a historical assessment, and no more names will be attached to it. The narrower, actionable statement is: the owner who actually holds the candidate path confirms whether to withdraw it and records rollback or recovery evidence. This page does not identify that owner, so the action cannot be assigned to a specific team.

This also means that success from application-events cannot be treated as authorization to withdraw the path. The entry point only answers for the behavior it observed; it cannot answer whether the candidate path is still in use. When responsibility for the candidate path is unconfirmed, the FAQ stops here rather than turning an unknown into a conclusion.

### Under what conditions can the work be closed?

The team retains the original wording: "Close work only when the native probe, neighboring client or host path, and rollback or recovery evidence agree on the same public behavior." This sentence is the only closure criterion on this page. All three types of evidence must point to the same public behavior. A passing native probe alone, or a neighboring path that merely appears normal, is not enough to close the work. If rollback or recovery evidence is missing, entry-point success cannot substitute for it either.

People still ask whether the Aspire resource graph can fill the gap in this assessment. The available material has no answer, and it does not assign the graph gap to the owner of SDK image refresh. That question remains unresolved.
